title: Adult day care in New York: social programs vs adult day health
seoTitle: Adult day care in NY: social vs adult day health care
seoDesc: How social adult day and adult day health care differ in New York, who regulates each, what Medicaid plans cover and how to find one in NYC or your county.
dek: Adult day care lets your parent spend the day somewhere safe and social, then sleep at home. New York has two very different kinds. Here is how they differ, who pays and how to find one.
keyFacts: Social adult day programs funded by an Office for the Aging follow NYSOFA rules. Adult day health care is regulated by the NYS Department of Health.
Under 10 NYCRR Part 425, each adult day health care session runs at least 5 hours, not counting travel, with at least one meal.
Medicaid managed long term care plans cover adult day health care, and can provide social day care as a care management service.
Every social adult day care in New York City must register with NYC Aging. Registration is not a license.
NY Connects routes you to local day programs: 1-800-342-9871.
body:
New York has two kinds of adult day care. Social adult day services give supervision, meals, activities and some personal care, under New York State Office for the Aging (NYSOFA) standards. Adult day health care adds nursing, therapy and health monitoring, and is regulated by the New York State Department of Health (DOH).

Both let your parent spend the day somewhere safe and social while you work or rest, then sleep at home. This guide explains the difference, who pays, how Medicaid plans cover each one and how to find and check a program in New York City and the rest of the state.

What is the difference between social adult day and adult day health care?

Social adult day services (SADS)Adult day health care (ADHC)
Who oversees itNYSOFA rules (Elder Law and 9 NYCRR 6654.20) for programs funded by an Office for the Aging; DOH requirements when paid by a Medicaid managed long term care plan; NYC Aging registration in the five boroughsDOH (10 NYCRR Part 425)
Who it servesPeople who need help with at least one daily activity, or supervision because of cognitive or psychosocial impairmentPeople with functional impairments who are not homebound and need supervision or monitoring, but not 24-hour inpatient care
Medical careNo nursing or therapy as a core serviceNursing, rehabilitation therapy, nutrition, social services, pharmacy services and more
How you get inContact the program or your local Office for the AgingA practitioner's order or a managed care plan referral, after a full assessment
Who usually runs itNonprofits, some county programs and private businessesA licensed nursing home, at the home or at an approved extension site
Ways to payPrivate pay, Office for the Aging funding, some MLTC plansMedicaid MLTC and MAP plans; ask the program about other ways to pay

What does a social adult day program offer?

NYSOFA describes social adult day services as long-term care for people with physical or cognitive impairments, under a person-centered service plan. Its stated goals include reducing loneliness, giving caregivers respite and helping working caregivers balance a job and caregiving.

NYSOFA lists four core services:

  • Socialization. Planned activities suited to each participant.
  • Monitoring and supervision. Including always knowing where each participant is.
  • Limited personal care. Help with mobility, toileting, transfers and eating.
  • Nutrition. Meals, snacks and drinks.

Programs may also offer fuller personal care (bathing, continence care, support with taking medications), practice with daily living skills, case assistance, caregiver services and transportation. Ask each program which of these it actually provides.

For a parent with dementia who is safe at home at night but can't be alone all day, a social program can be a good fit. NYSOFA says people who need supervision because of cognitive impairment are eligible. Our memory care guide covers other dementia options.

A good day program can give your parent company and give you back a workday.

What does adult day health care offer?

Adult day health care is a health program run in a group setting for people with functional impairments who live in the community. Under DOH's regulation (10 NYCRR Part 425, effective March 20, 2024), every program must have at least these available: case management, health education, care planning, nursing, nutrition, social services, help and supervision with daily activities like toileting, eating, walking and bathing, rehabilitation and maintenance therapy, planned activities, pharmacy services and referrals for dental and specialist care.

Each session must run at least five hours, not counting travel, and must include at least one meal plus snacks and drinks. The program, or the plan that referred your parent, must keep assessing each person's health. A single visit can be shorter or longer than five hours, depending on the person's needs.

ADHC suits a parent who needs regular nursing attention (wound care, medication monitoring, therapy after a stroke) but still lives at home and is not homebound. After a hospital stay, ask the hospital discharge planner whether a program could help.

Who pays for adult day care in New York?

It depends on the type of program and your parent's coverage.

  • Medicaid managed long term care (MLTC). DOH lists adult day health care as a covered service in MLTC plans, and social day care as one of the care management services a plan can provide. Medicaid Advantage Plus (MAP) plans also include ADHC. See our MLTC guide to learn who must enroll and how plans authorize services.
  • PACE. Where it operates, PACE can include adult day primary care, with meals and recreational therapy, according to Medicare.gov.
  • Office for the Aging funding. NYSOFA gives grants to 12 social adult day organizations directly, and says local Offices for the Aging fund about 52 more. Ask the county office whether your parent qualifies for a funded spot.
  • Private pay. Families can pay a program directly. Rates vary by program and region, so ask for the daily rate, what it includes and whether transportation costs extra.
  • Medicare. Medicare.gov lists adult day health care as a kind of long-term care and says Medicare doesn't pay for long-term care. Don't count on Medicare to pay for a day program.

If your parent might qualify for Medicaid, read our Medicaid guide. If they don't qualify, the EISEP program and other caregiver support through the county may help fill gaps.

How do I find an adult day program in New York City?

In the five boroughs, every social adult day care must register with NYC Aging under the city's Administrative Code before it operates. Programs must also follow NYSOFA program standards and participant rights and the city's rules in Chapter 2 of Title 69 of the Rules of the City of New York.

NYC Aging says registration does not grant a license or certification, and it does not judge the quality of services. It can investigate complaints and issue violations. Each program must post a sign with the contact for the SADC Ombuds Office and a participant rights sign.

  • Search registered programs with NYC Aging's social adult day care search tool.
  • Read NYC Aging's guide to choosing a social adult day care on its social adult day care page.
  • Make a complaint online or by calling 311.

For adult day health care in the city, ask your parent's MLTC plan for its contracted programs, or ask the hospital discharge planner.

How do I find a program outside New York City?

  1. Call NY Connects. Dial 1-800-342-9871 and name your parent's county. NY Connects links you to local long-term care services, including day programs.
  2. Contact the county Office for the Aging. Find it on NYSOFA's local offices page. Ask which social adult day programs it funds and whether your parent qualifies.
  3. Ask the Medicaid plan. If your parent is in an MLTC, MAP or PACE plan, ask the care manager which day programs are in the network and how to get the service authorized.
  4. Get the right order for ADHC. Adult day health care needs a practitioner's order or a managed care plan referral, plus a comprehensive assessment by the program or the plan.
  5. Visit on a normal day. Stay for lunch and an activity. Watch how staff speak to participants.
  6. Try a trial period. Ask whether your parent can start with one or two days a week while everyone adjusts.

How does a day program fit with other caregiver help?

A day program covers the daytime. For nights, weekends or a longer break, New York has other respite options. NYSOFA says the aging services network supports caregivers directly with programs such as respite, and 17 counties have NYSOFA-funded Caregiver Resource Centers with support groups, counseling and training. For families caring for someone with dementia, DOH funds Alzheimer's Disease Regional Caregiver Support Initiative programs that offer caregiver assessments, support groups and respite, including overnight respite. The Alzheimer's Association 24-hour helpline, listed by DOH, is 1-800-272-3900.

Licensed adult care facilities can also offer short respite stays. The state's Health Profiles site says respite in these facilities can last up to 120 days in any 12-month period. Our caregiver support guide pulls these options together, and our assisted living guide explains the facilities.

What should I ask before choosing a day program?

  • Is this a social adult day program or adult day health care? Who oversees you?
  • In New York City, are you registered with NYC Aging?
  • What are your hours and days? What happens if I'm late for pickup?
  • Do you provide transportation? What area does it cover, and how long is the ride?
  • What personal care can staff give (toileting, help with meals, bathing)?
  • How do you handle a participant with dementia who becomes upset or tries to leave?
  • Who gives medications, and how are they recorded?
  • Which Medicaid plans do you contract with? What is the private daily rate, and what's included?
  • How will you tell me about falls, illness or changes you notice?
Day care and home care can work together

You can pair a day program with a few hours of help at home in the morning or evening. See our guides to home care agencies and CDPAP.

faq.q: How do I find adult day care for my mom with dementia in Staten Island?
faq.a: Search NYC Aging's social adult day care search tool for registered programs on Staten Island, and read NYC Aging's guide to choosing one. Ask how staff handle participants with dementia. If she has a Medicaid managed long term care plan, ask the care manager which social or adult day health programs are in the network.

faq.q: Will Medicaid pay for adult day care for my dad in Nassau County?
faq.a: If he is in a Medicaid managed long term care plan, adult day health care is a covered service, and social day care can be provided as a care management service. The plan must authorize it. If he is not on Medicaid, call NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871 or the Nassau County Office for the Aging about funded programs.

faq.q: What is the difference between social adult day care and adult day health care?
faq.a: Social adult day gives supervision, socialization, meals and limited personal care under NYSOFA standards. Adult day health care is regulated by the Department of Health and adds nursing, therapy, pharmacy and other health services, with sessions of at least five hours.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for adult day care?
faq.a: Medicare.gov lists adult day health care as long-term care and says Medicare doesn't pay for long-term care, so families should not count on Medicare to pay for a day program. Medicaid plans, PACE, Office for the Aging funding or private pay are the usual routes.

faq.q: Who qualifies for a social adult day program in New York?
faq.a: NYSOFA says a person is eligible if they need help from another person with at least one daily activity, such as toileting, mobility, transferring or eating, or need supervision because of cognitive or psychosocial impairment.

faq.q: How do I complain about a social adult day care in NYC?
faq.a: Submit a comment or complaint to NYC Aging online or call 311. Every registered program must post a sign with the contact for NYC Aging's SADC Ombuds Office and a sign listing participants' rights.

title: Assisted living in New York: licenses, costs and how to check
seoTitle: Assisted living in NY: ALR, EALR, SNALR and who pays
seoDesc: How New York licenses assisted living (adult homes, ALR, EALR, SNALR), who pays, how the Medicaid ALP works and how to check a residence on the state site.
dek: In New York, the license on the wall decides who a residence can admit and whether your parent can stay as needs grow. Here is what each license means, who pays and how to check a place before you sign.
keyFacts: NY DOH licenses adult homes, enriched housing and residences for adults. These are not licensed for continual nursing care.
An Enhanced ALR (EALR) can keep residents who need help walking or have unmanaged incontinence. A Special Needs ALR (SNALR) serves people with dementia.
Medicare.gov says Medicare and Medigap don't pay for long-term care, including non-medical care in assisted living.
2026 SSI for an adult care facility resident on SSI only: $1,688 a month, with at least $262 kept as a personal needs allowance (DOH).
DOH adult care facility complaint line: 1-866-893-6772, 8:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. weekdays.
body:
Assisted living in New York means a licensed adult care facility that gives housing, meals, 24-hour supervision and help with daily tasks, but not round-the-clock nursing. The state licenses several kinds (adult homes, enriched housing and assisted living residences), and the license tells you who a place may admit and how long your parent can stay as needs grow.

That second point matters more than the brochure, the dining room or the view. This guide explains each license in plain words, who pays, how the Medicaid Assisted Living Program works and how to check any residence on the state's own site before you sign.

What kinds of assisted living does New York license?

The New York State Department of Health (DOH) licenses adult care facilities, which give long-term, non-medical residential care to adults who cannot live fully on their own. DOH says these facilities are not licensed to give continual medical or nursing care. The main types are:

  • Adult home. Room, board, housekeeping, personal care and supervision for five or more unrelated adults.
  • Enriched housing program. Long-term care for five or more adults, mainly 65 and older, in settings that look more like regular apartments. It provides or arranges room, board, housekeeping, personal care and supervision.
  • Residence for adults. Room, board, housekeeping, case management, activities and supervision for five or more adults who cannot live on their own. Personal care is not on DOH's list of its services.

On top of those, a facility can hold an Assisted Living Residence (ALR) license. The state's Health Profiles site says an ALR gives housing, on-site monitoring and personal or home care in a home-like setting, and it must sit within a licensed adult home or enriched housing program. An ALR can then add one or both of two extra certifications.

License or certificationWhat it allows (per DOH and NYS Health Profiles)
Basic Assisted Living Residence (ALR)Daily food service, 24-hour on-site monitoring, case management and an individualized service plan for each resident
Enhanced Assisted Living Residence (EALR)Can admit or keep residents who chronically need help walking or using stairs, depend on medical equipment that needs frequent staff help, or have chronic unmanaged bladder or bowel incontinence
Special Needs Assisted Living Residence (SNALR)Serves residents with special needs, including dementia or other cognitive impairment
Assisted Living Program (ALP)Offered by some adult homes and enriched housing programs for people who medically qualify for a nursing home but can do well in a less intensive setting
Respite careTemporary stays of up to 120 days in any 12-month period while a caregiver gets a break

"Independent senior housing" is a different thing. A 2016 DOH letter explains that it is not licensed by DOH. The housing provider may give residents a list of agencies but cannot provide, arrange or coordinate personal care. With limited exceptions, a building that offers 24-hour supervision, medication management or help with bathing and dressing needs a DOH license.

Ask which license the building holds before you ask about the menu.

Why does the license type matter so much?

The license decides whether your parent can stay when their health changes. A basic ALR has limits on who it can keep. If your mom starts needing help to walk most of the time or develops incontinence she can't manage, a basic ALR may have to ask her to move. An EALR is built for that kind of aging in place.

Dementia works the same way. A residence needs SNALR certification to serve people with dementia, and a 2016 DOH letter says a SNALR must have a special needs plan showing how residents' needs will be safely met. The same letter says one operator can hold both EALR and SNALR certification. If your dad has early memory loss, ask now whether the building has SNALR beds, so a second move later is less likely. Our memory care guide covers this in more depth.

Some limits apply everywhere in adult care. Under the Assisted Living Program rules, DOH says people may not be admitted if they need continual nursing care, are chronically bedfast or are impaired to a degree that endangers other residents. For those needs, a nursing home is usually the setting. See our nursing home ratings guide.

Who pays for assisted living in New York?

Most families pay privately. Medicare.gov says Medicare and most health insurance, including Medigap, don't pay for long-term care, and it lists assisted living as one of the places that non-medical long-term care happens. Medicare.gov points to Medicaid or private long-term care insurance as the other ways to pay.

There are three main kinds of public help:

  • SSI and the state supplement. DOH says adult homes and enriched housing are available through Supplemental Security Income (SSI) or private payment. Residents of adult care facilities who get SSI receive a higher combined federal and state amount than someone living at home.
  • Medicaid Assisted Living Program (ALP). For people who qualify for a nursing home but can live in a lower-cost setting. More on this below.
  • The SNALR voucher program. A limited state program for people with dementia who can no longer afford private pay. Details are in our memory care guide.
2026 SSI for an adult care facility residentMonthly SSI (federal and state)
Individual, SSI only$1,688
Individual, SSI plus Social Security or other unearned income$1,708
Couple, SSI only$3,376
Minimum personal needs allowance (individual)$262

These figures come from DOH's January 2026 letter to adult care facility operators (DAL 25-08). The personal needs allowance is money the resident keeps for personal items such as clothing. The same letter says a facility must give SSI residents at least 30 days' written notice before raising its rate, and an ALR must give 45 days. SSI amounts change each January, so check the Office of Temporary and Disability Assistance (OTDA) or DOH for 2027 figures.

Private rates vary by building, region and level of care. Ask every residence for its full rate sheet in writing, including what costs extra. The DOH Assisted Living Residence Quality site posts the cost of rent and a summary of services for each ALR.

How does the Medicaid Assisted Living Program (ALP) work?

The ALP lets a person who medically qualifies for a nursing home live in an adult home or enriched housing program instead, with extra services. DOH lists those services as personal care, room and board, housekeeping, supervision, home health aides, a personal emergency response system, nursing, physical, occupational and speech therapy, medical supplies and equipment, adult day health care, home health services and case management by a registered nurse.

DOH says both Medicaid members and private payers can use an ALP if they are medically eligible for nursing home placement and would otherwise need it because they lack a home or a suitable home setting. For Medicaid questions, contact the Human Resources Administration (HRA) in New York City or the county Department of Social Services elsewhere.

The ALP sits outside managed long term care. DOH lists the Assisted Living Program as a service excluded from MLTC plan coverage, and residents of an ALP are excluded from MLTC enrollment. Our managed long term care guide explains the rest. If your parent is not on Medicaid yet, start with our Medicaid guide.

Not every building has ALP beds

Only some adult homes and enriched housing programs run an ALP. The NYS Health Profiles site lets you search adult care facilities by service, so you can find the ones that list the Assisted Living Program.

How do I check an assisted living residence in New York?

Use two free state tools before you tour.

  • NYS Health Profiles: Adult Care Facilities lets you search by name, county, region, facility type or service, such as EALR, SNALR or ALP. It also has a printable directory of every adult care facility.
  • Assisted Living Residence Quality was created after a February 14, 2025 change to state law. For each ALR it posts the website, address, cost of rent, a summary of services and the approved residency agreement template. It also shows three quality measures: confirmed complaints in 2025, average direct care staffing (self-reported by the facility) and food service violations from the latest recertification survey.
  1. Look up the license. Search the facility on NYS Health Profiles. Note whether it is an adult home or enriched housing program, and whether it lists ALR, EALR, SNALR or ALP.
  2. Read the residency agreement. Download it from the ALR Quality site. Look for what triggers a move-out, how rates rise and what notice is required.
  3. Check complaints, food citations and staffing. Compare a few residences on the same page.
  4. Tour twice. Go once at a mealtime and once in the evening or on a weekend, when staffing is thinner.
  5. Ask about the ombudsman. The Long Term Care Ombudsman Program serves residents of assisted living and other licensed adult care homes. Ask how residents reach theirs.
  6. Get everything in writing. Rates, extra fees, what happens if needs increase and how much notice either side must give.

What questions should I ask on a tour?

  • Which licenses and certifications do you hold: ALR, EALR, SNALR, ALP?
  • If my mother's needs increase, at what point would she have to move? Can she move to an enhanced or special needs unit here?
  • Who manages medications, and how are they stored and recorded?
  • How many direct care staff are on each shift, including overnight?
  • What is included in the monthly rate, and what costs extra (laundry, escorts to appointments, extra care hours)?
  • How often have rates gone up in recent years, and how much notice do you give?
  • Do you accept SSI? Do you have ALP beds, and is there a wait?
  • How do you handle a fall or a trip to the hospital, and is the room held?

Bring a copy of your parent's health care proxy and power of attorney. The residence will ask who can make decisions and who signs the agreement.

Where do I complain about an assisted living residence?

Call the DOH Centralized Complaint Intake Program for Adult Care Facilities at 1-866-893-6772. DOH says it answers 8:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. weekdays, excluding holidays. After hours you can leave a voicemail, and DOH says those calls are addressed within one to two business days. You can stay anonymous, but give as much detail as you can: the facility name and address, who was involved and when it happened.

The Long Term Care Ombudsman Program advocates for residents of nursing homes, assisted living and other licensed adult care homes. Ombudsmen investigate complaints, mediate among residents, families and staff, and refer problems to DOH when they can't be resolved. Call 1-855-582-6769 or find the local ombudsman at ltcombudsman.ny.gov. If you suspect abuse or financial exploitation, also see our Adult Protective Services guide.

If assisted living isn't the right fit yet, help at home may be. See our guides to home care agencies, adult day care and NY Connects (1-800-342-9871), which can walk you through local options in any county.

faq.q: How do I find assisted living for my mom in Westchester that can handle dementia?
faq.a: Search NYS Health Profiles: Adult Care Facilities by county (Westchester) and by the service Special Needs Assisted Living Residence. A residence needs SNALR certification to serve people with dementia. Then compare rent, services and quality measures on the DOH Assisted Living Residence Quality site, and tour.

faq.q: Will Medicaid pay for assisted living for my dad in Queens?
faq.a: Medicaid's main route is the Assisted Living Program (ALP). If he medically qualifies for a nursing home, an ALP in a participating adult home or enriched housing program can provide nursing, therapy, personal care and other services. Ask HRA about Medicaid in New York City. Residents on SSI also get a higher SSI amount in adult care facilities.

faq.q: What is the difference between an ALR and an EALR in New York?
faq.a: A basic Assisted Living Residence gives daily food service, 24-hour on-site monitoring, case management and an individualized service plan. An Enhanced ALR can also admit or keep residents who chronically need help walking or using stairs, depend on medical equipment that needs frequent help from medical staff, or have chronic unmanaged incontinence.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for assisted living?
faq.a: No. Medicare.gov says Medicare and most health insurance, including Medigap, don't pay for long-term care, and it lists assisted living as one place where that non-medical care happens. Medicaid or private long-term care insurance may help.

faq.q: How can I check inspections or complaints about an assisted living residence?
faq.a: Look up the facility on NYS Health Profiles: Adult Care Facilities, and check the DOH Assisted Living Residence Quality page for confirmed complaints, staffing, food citations and the residency agreement. To report a problem, call the DOH complaint line at 1-866-893-6772 or the Long Term Care Ombudsman Program at 1-855-582-6769.

faq.q: Is independent senior housing the same as assisted living?
faq.a: No. A 2016 DOH letter says independent senior housing is not licensed by DOH. The housing provider may hand residents a list of outside agencies but cannot provide, arrange or coordinate personal care. A building that offers services like 24-hour supervision, personal care or medication management generally needs a DOH license.

title: CDPAP in New York: how family caregivers get paid in 2026
seoTitle: CDPAP in NY 2026: who qualifies and how family gets paid
seoDesc: New York's CDPAP lets Medicaid members hire a relative or friend as a paid aide. Who qualifies, who cannot be hired, how PPL works and how to enroll in 2026.
dek: The Consumer Directed Personal Assistance Program lets a New Yorker on Medicaid choose their own home care aide, often an adult child or other relative. Since 2025 every case runs through one statewide payroll company. Here is how it works now.
keyFacts: CDPAP is a New York Medicaid program. The person getting care, or their designated representative, hires and supervises the aide.
Adult children, other relatives and friends can be hired. A spouse, the designated representative and the parent of a consumer under 21 cannot.
Public Partnerships LLC (PPL) is the only statewide fiscal intermediary. PPL: 1-833-247-5346, TTY 1-833-204-9042.
For assessments on or after September 1, 2025, adults must meet new minimum needs requirements.
Initial Medicaid home care assessments are scheduled through the New York Independent Assessor at 1-855-222-8350.
body:
The Consumer Directed Personal Assistance Program (CDPAP) is a New York Medicaid program that lets an eligible person hire their own home care aide, and that aide can be an adult child, another relative or a friend. Since 2025, every CDPAP aide in the state is paid through one company, Public Partnerships LLC (PPL), the Statewide Fiscal Intermediary.

For many families this is how a daughter or son gets paid for the care they are already giving. The rules are specific, though, and they changed in 2025. This guide sticks to what the New York State Department of Health (DOH) says on its own pages.

What is CDPAP, and how is it different from regular home care?

With regular Medicaid home care, an agency hires, trains and schedules the aide. With CDPAP, the person receiving care, called the consumer, is in charge. The aide is called a personal assistant.

That control comes with real responsibilities. DOH says the consumer, or their designated representative, must handle:

  • Recruiting, hiring, training and supervising personal assistants
  • Ending employment when needed
  • Arranging backup coverage when the assistant is sick or away
  • Coordinating other services
  • Keeping payroll records and working with the fiscal intermediary to process payroll

If your parent cannot do these things, a designated representative can make the decisions for them. That is often another family member. The designated representative cannot also be the paid assistant.

Who qualifies for CDPAP?

According to DOH, a person must:

  • Be eligible for New York State Medicaid
  • Have a stable medical condition
  • Have a home care need found through a state-approved assessment
  • Meet the Minimum Needs Requirements if they are 21 or older
  • Be able to direct their own care, or have a designated representative who can

What are the Minimum Needs Requirements?

These apply to assessments done on or after September 1, 2025. An adult must need one of the following:

  • Standard rule. At least limited assistance with physical maneuvering with more than two activities of daily living.
  • Dementia or Alzheimer's. With a diagnosis of dementia or Alzheimer's disease, at least supervision with more than one activity of daily living.

DOH lists exemptions for PACE enrollment (PACE is the all-inclusive care program for people 55 and older) and for people who were already authorized for or receiving personal care or CDPAP services, or were continuously enrolled in a managed long-term care (MLTC) plan, as of September 1, 2025.

Medicaid eligibility itself has income and asset rules. Our Medicaid for older New Yorkers guide explains them.

CDPAP pays for care your parent is assessed to need. It does not pay a relative for every hour they spend helping.

Who can be the paid caregiver?

DOH says friends and family can be hired as personal assistants, with three exceptions:

Can be hiredCannot be hired
Adult childrenThe consumer's spouse
Siblings, nieces, nephews, grandchildren and other relativesThe consumer's designated representative
Friends and neighborsThe parent of a consumer under age 21

So if your mom is the one who needs care, you can be her paid assistant, but your dad (her husband) cannot. If your brother is her designated representative, he cannot also be paid as her assistant. Many families split the roles so one person directs care and another provides it.

A state policy issued July 22, 2026 also flags personal assistants who work 112 or more hours in a single week. Plans must then contact the consumer or designated representative and check that there are enough assistants and informal supports to meet program rules. If there are not, the plan can end the current authorization, with notice, and arrange other supports. If one relative is covering nearly every hour, line up a second assistant early.

What changed in 2025 with PPL?

Before 2025, hundreds of local companies acted as fiscal intermediaries, handling payroll for CDPAP aides. New York replaced them with one Statewide Fiscal Intermediary, Public Partnerships LLC (PPL). DOH now says all CDPAP recipients are required to work with PPL as their fiscal intermediary, which processes payroll for personal assistants.

DateWhat happened (per DOH)
February 4, 2025Commissioner's letter told consumers to move to PPL by March 28, 2025, and said they could keep their caregiver.
March 27, 2025DOH announced a late registration window through April 30 for current consumers and workers, with retroactive pay for April hours once registered.
May 19, 2025About 280,000 people were authorized for CDPAP before April 1. 209,000 who remained authorized had registered with PPL. About 75,000 moved to Personal Care Services instead.
June 6, 2025Under a federal court agreement, certain assistants could be paid by their old fiscal intermediary until this date.
September 1, 2025Minimum Needs Requirements took effect for assessments and reassessments.
October 23, 2025DOH announced that the Appellate Division, First Department, upheld the award of the statewide fiscal intermediary contract to PPL.
July 22, 2026MLTC Policy 26.02 on excessive hours (112 or more a week) took effect.

DOH said in 2025 that CDPAP eligibility was not changing because of the switch, and consumers could keep their trusted caregiver as long as that caregiver also moved to PPL. DOH also said PPL offers assistants a benefits package that includes paid time off, holiday pay, overtime, medical coverage, a retirement savings plan, ongoing professional development and family leave. Assistants whose consumers live in the Bronx, Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, Staten Island, Nassau, Suffolk or Westchester also get a flex card for health-related costs.

If your family switched to agency care

DOH said in May 2025 that some people may register with PPL and later switch to Personal Care Services, or the other way around. If your family wants to move back to CDPAP, call your plan or local Department of Social Services first.

How do I enroll my parent in CDPAP?

The path depends on if your parent already has Medicaid home care.

  1. Get Medicaid in place. In New York City, Medicaid is handled by the Human Resources Administration (HRA). Elsewhere, it is the county Department of Social Services. NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871 can help with the application.
  2. Request a home care assessment. Call the New York Independent Assessor Program at 1-855-222-8350 (TTY 1-888-329-1541). If your parent is already in a Medicaid managed care plan, call the plan instead. The Community Health Assessment usually takes 2 to 3 hours, and the clinical appointment up to 1 hour. Both can be in person or by video.
  3. Say you want consumer directed services. Tell the assessor, plan or county that your parent wants CDPAP and who will be the assistant. If your parent needs a managed long-term care plan, New York Medicaid Choice at 1-888-401-6582 helps with enrollment.
  4. Register with PPL. Both your parent and the assistant register with PPL at 1-833-247-5346 (TTY 1-833-204-9042) or online at PPL's New York CDPAP page. DOH says there is no cost.
  5. Get help if you need it. DOH lets consumers who want help request a CDPAP facilitator using the Optional Facilitator Selection Form on the DOH CDPAP page.
  6. Submit timesheets. DOH said in May 2025 that PPL pays assistants weekly based on timesheets submitted to PPL. Almost all assistants who had not been paid had not submitted a timesheet.

What do you need to register with PPL?

The DOH letter lists your parent's address and contact information, date of birth, Medicaid number and the caregiver's information. DOH said you will not need bank account or credit card details over the phone. Treat anyone who asks for those on a cold call as a possible scam.

Who do I call with a problem?

  • PPL for registration, timesheets and pay: 1-833-247-5346
  • DOH, if your parent is in a managed care plan: 1-866-712-7197
  • DOH, if your parent is not in managed care and works with the local Department of Social Services: 518-474-5888
  • DOH email: StatewideFI@health.ny.gov

In March 2025, DOH said it had sent cease and desist letters to fiscal intermediaries and licensed home care agencies over false or coercive information about CDPAP. If a company calls promising to keep you in CDPAP for a fee, check with PPL or DOH before you sign anything.

What mistakes should families avoid?

  • Making the spouse the paid assistant. Spouses cannot be hired. Another relative or a friend can.
  • Naming the paid assistant as designated representative. These must be two different people.
  • Having no backup. The consumer must arrange coverage. A second registered assistant protects your parent if the main one gets sick.
  • Skipping timesheets. No timesheet, no paycheck.
  • Assuming Medicare pays. CDPAP is Medicaid. Medicare does not provide long-term or custodial care unless medical care is needed.

If your parent does not qualify for Medicaid, ask your county Office for the Aging about the Expanded In-home Services program (EISEP), and read our home care agencies guide before hiring privately.

faq.q: Can I get paid to take care of my mom in Brooklyn?
faq.a: Possibly, through CDPAP, if your mom has New York Medicaid and is assessed as needing home care. Adult children can be hired as personal assistants. In NYC, Medicaid goes through HRA. Request the home care assessment through the New York Independent Assessor at 1-855-222-8350, or through her Medicaid plan.

faq.q: Can my dad hire me as his aide in Rochester if my mother is his wife?
faq.a: Yes, you can be hired, but your mother cannot, because spouses are excluded. The designated representative also cannot be the paid assistant. Your dad needs Medicaid and an assessment showing he needs home care.

faq.q: Can a spouse be paid through CDPAP in New York?
faq.a: No. DOH lists the consumer's spouse, the designated representative and the parent of a consumer under 21 as people who cannot be hired as personal assistants.

faq.q: What is PPL in CDPAP?
faq.a: Public Partnerships LLC is New York's Statewide Fiscal Intermediary for CDPAP. All CDPAP recipients must work with PPL. It processes payroll for personal assistants and offers them a benefits package. Call 1-833-247-5346.

faq.q: Does my parent qualify for CDPAP with dementia?
faq.a: For assessments on or after September 1, 2025, an adult with a dementia or Alzheimer's diagnosis must need at least supervision with more than one activity of daily living, and must meet the other CDPAP rules, including Medicaid eligibility. If they cannot direct their own care, a designated representative must do it for them.

faq.q: Do we have to pay to register with PPL?
faq.a: No. DOH says there is no cost to register with PPL, and you will not be asked for bank account or credit card details over the phone.

title: Home care agencies in New York: how to choose and check them
seoTitle: Home care agencies in NY: LHCSA, CHHA and how to check
seoDesc: How NY home care agencies differ, what Medicare and Medicaid pay for, how to check an agency and aide with the state, and where to complain if care goes wrong.
dek: Before a stranger comes into your parent's home, it helps to know which kind of agency you are dealing with, who is paying and how to check them. A plain guide to LHCSAs, CHHAs, private aides and the state tools that let you verify them.
keyFacts: Certified Home Health Agencies (CHHAs) give part-time skilled care and can bill Medicare and Medicaid. Licensed Home Care Services Agencies (LHCSAs) mostly serve private-pay clients.
Since January 1, 2019, a LHCSA must be registered with the NYS Department of Health before it operates.
Medicare pays $0 for covered home health if your parent is homebound and needs part-time skilled care. It does not pay for 24-hour care or personal care alone.
The NYS Home Care Registry lets you look up home health and personal care aides who finished state-approved training, by name or registry number.
DOH Home Health Hotline for complaints: 1-800-628-5972, staffed 8:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. weekdays.
body:
New York has two main kinds of home care agency, and the difference decides who pays. Certified Home Health Agencies (CHHAs) provide part-time skilled care that Medicare and Medicaid can pay for, while Licensed Home Care Services Agencies (LHCSAs) mostly provide aides for families paying privately or for patients whose care another provider manages.

Both are overseen by the New York State Department of Health (DOH). Both can be checked online. This guide explains how, plus what to ask and where to complain.

What is the difference between a LHCSA and a CHHA?

Certified Home Health Agency (CHHA)Licensed Home Care Services Agency (LHCSA)
Main jobPart-time, intermittent skilled care at homeHome care services, mostly for clients who pay privately
ServicesNursing, home health aides, and medical supplies and equipment, plus at least one more serviceAides and nurses. May work under contract, for example sending a home health aide to a CHHA patient.
Who paysMedicare, Medicaid, private insurance or private payMostly private pay or private insurance. Serves Medicare or Medicaid patients under contract when another provider or plan manages the case.
State oversightDOH surveys and complaint investigationsDOH registration (required since January 1, 2019), surveys and complaint investigations

In practice, a CHHA is often what shows up after a hospital stay, when a doctor orders nursing and therapy at home. A LHCSA is usually who you call when you want an aide for bathing, dressing, meals or company a few hours a day and plan to pay for it yourself.

When DOH finds violations at either type, it issues a Statement of Deficiencies. The agency must submit a plan of correction within 10 days.

What does Medicare pay for at home?

Medicare covers home health care, which is short-term skilled care. It does not cover ongoing help with daily life. According to Medicare.gov, your parent qualifies when:

  • They need part-time or intermittent skilled care, such as nursing or therapy.
  • They are homebound. Leaving home takes a lot of effort, they have trouble leaving without help, or leaving is not recommended because of their condition. Leaving for medical treatment, adult day care or short, infrequent outings does not break this rule.
  • A doctor or other allowed provider has seen them in person and ordered the care.
  • A Medicare-certified home health agency provides it.

Part-time or intermittent usually means skilled nursing and aide care combined of up to 8 hours a day and 28 hours a week. If the provider decides it is necessary, that can be less than 8 hours a day and up to 35 hours a week.

ItemWhat your parent pays under Original Medicare
Covered home health services$0
Medicare-covered medical equipment20% of the Medicare-approved amount after the Part B deductible
24-hour care, meal delivery, homemaker services, or personal care aloneNot covered

Before giving services or supplies Medicare will not cover, the agency should give your parent a written Advance Beneficiary Notice (ABN). If your parent has a Medicare Advantage plan, the plan's rules and network apply. Our Medicare costs guide has the 2027 deductibles.

Medicare is built for recovery. Medicaid is what pays for long-term help at home.

What does Medicaid pay for?

Medicaid is the main public payer for long-term home care in New York. Once your parent has Medicaid and is assessed as needing help, options include agency Personal Care Services or the Consumer Directed Personal Assistance Program (CDPAP), where your parent hires their own aide, sometimes a relative.

  • Initial assessments for personal care and CDPAP are scheduled through the New York Independent Assessor Program at 1-855-222-8350.
  • Managed long-term care plans are for people assessed as needing community-based long-term care for more than 120 days. New York Medicaid Choice helps with enrollment at 1-888-401-6582.
  • In New York City, Medicaid applications go through the Human Resources Administration (HRA). Elsewhere, they go through the county Department of Social Services.

Our Medicaid guide covers eligibility. If your parent does not qualify, ask the county Office for the Aging about EISEP, or call NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871.

How do I check an agency and an aide?

  1. Look up the agency. Search DOH's Home Health and Hospice Profiles by name, county or type. You can see inspection information and, for certified agencies, quality measures such as patient satisfaction, managing pain and preventing unplanned hospital care.
  2. Check the type. Confirm whether it is a CHHA or a LHCSA, and that it serves your parent's county. If you want Medicare to pay, it must be Medicare-certified.
  3. Look up the aide. Search the New York State Home Care Registry by name (at least two letters of the last name) or by registry number. It gives limited information on home health aides and personal care aides who finished a state-approved training program.
  4. Read the registry carefully. DOH says most of the information is reported by the workers themselves, certifications may have lapsed and some data may be out of date. DOH urges reference checks on anyone you are thinking of hiring, especially anyone whose employment status is not "YES."
  5. Ask about the criminal history check. State law (Public Health Law section 2899-a) requires home care agencies to request a criminal history check through DOH for prospective employees covered by the law. An agency can give temporary approval while a check is pending only with direct observation of the worker. Agencies cannot charge workers for the check.

If you hire an aide privately, without an agency, none of these agency checks happen automatically. You become the employer. Check references yourself and ask a tax professional about household employer rules.

How is home care different in New York City?

The agency rules are the same statewide. The same DOH Profiles site, Home Care Registry and complaint line cover the five boroughs and the rest of the state. What changes is who handles Medicaid.

  • In the five boroughs, Medicaid applications go through the Human Resources Administration (HRA). NYC Aging runs NY Connects through a partner agency in each borough, and its Aging Connect line is 212-244-6469.
  • Everywhere else, Medicaid goes through the county Department of Social Services, and the county Office for the Aging is the local hub for non-Medicaid help.

Many agencies serve only some counties. A Long Island agency may not cover Queens, and a Buffalo agency may not cover rural Erie County towns. Ask before you sign.

Planning for a hospital discharge

Most families first meet a home care agency when a parent leaves the hospital or rehab. Before discharge, ask the hospital social worker or discharge planner:

  • Has the doctor ordered home health care, and which Medicare-certified agency will come?
  • When will the first nurse or therapist visit?
  • What equipment is being ordered, like a walker, shower chair or hospital bed?
  • Who do we call if no one shows up in the first two days?
  • When skilled care ends, what help is there for bathing and meals?

That last question matters most. Medicare home health stops when skilled care is no longer needed, even if your parent still needs help with daily tasks. Planning the next step early avoids a gap.

What should I ask a home care agency?

  • Are you a CHHA or a LHCSA? Can I see your DOH license or registration?
  • Are your aides employees of the agency? Who pays their taxes and workers' compensation?
  • Are all aides on the Home Care Registry? Have they cleared the criminal history check?
  • Who supervises aides, and how often does a nurse visit?
  • What happens if the aide is sick or does not show up? How fast do you send a replacement?
  • Can we meet the aide first, and can we ask for a different one?
  • What is the hourly rate, the minimum shift and any extra charge for nights, weekends or holidays?
  • Do you accept my parent's Medicaid plan or long-term care insurance?
  • How do I raise a complaint with the agency itself?

What are the red flags?

  • The agency does not appear on DOH's Profiles site, or the name does not match.
  • They will not tell you whether they are a CHHA or a LHCSA.
  • They want cash only, or large payments up front.
  • The aide is not on the Home Care Registry and the agency cannot explain why.
  • No one supervises the aide or returns your calls.
  • The aide asks your parent for money, gifts, bank cards or passwords, or pressures them to sign anything.
  • Someone calls offering to "sign your parent up" for Medicaid home care for a fee.
If you suspect abuse or theft

Call 911 if your parent is in danger. For neglect, abuse or financial exploitation by anyone, see our Adult Protective Services guide.

How do I complain to the Department of Health?

DOH runs the federally mandated Home Health Hotline at 1-800-628-5972. DOH says it can be called 24 hours a day, seven days a week, and staff answer from 8:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m., Monday through Friday. You can also complain in writing.

  • Email: HomeHospiceCCIP@health.ny.gov
  • Fax: 518-408-1157
  • Mail: Division of Home and Community Based Services, CCIP, 875 Central Avenue, Albany, NY 12206
  • More details: on the DOH complaints page

Describe what happened, when and the agency's name. Your name and contact details are optional, but they let DOH follow up. For general home care questions, the Division of Home and Community Based Services is at 518-408-1638 or homecare@health.ny.gov.

Keep a simple log of visits, missed shifts and concerns. It makes any complaint easier to investigate.

faq.q: How do I find a licensed home care agency for my dad in Westchester?
faq.a: Search the NYS DOH Home Health and Hospice Profiles site by county and agency type. It shows CHHAs and LHCSAs, inspection information and, for certified agencies, quality measures. Then confirm the agency's registration and ask the questions in this guide.

faq.q: Will Medicare pay for an aide for my mom in the Bronx after her hospital stay?
faq.a: Medicare covers home health aide care only while she also gets skilled care, such as nursing or therapy, is homebound and has a provider's order. It does not cover 24-hour care or personal care alone. For ongoing help, look at Medicaid home care or private pay.

faq.q: What is a LHCSA in New York?
faq.a: A Licensed Home Care Services Agency offers home care services, mostly to people who pay privately or have private insurance. It can also serve Medicare or Medicaid patients under contract with another provider. Since January 1, 2019, it must be registered with the Department of Health to operate.

faq.q: How do I check if a home health aide is certified in New York?
faq.a: Search the NYS Home Care Registry by name or registry number. It lists aides who finished state-approved training. DOH warns that some entries may be outdated, so also check references.

faq.q: Where do I report a bad home care agency in New York?
faq.a: Call the DOH Home Health Hotline at 1-800-628-5972 (staffed 8:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. weekdays), email HomeHospiceCCIP@health.ny.gov, or write to the address on the complaints page of the DOH Profiles site.

faq.q: Do New York home care aides get background checks?
faq.a: State law requires home care agencies to request a criminal history check through DOH for covered prospective employees. Ask the agency to confirm the check was completed. Families hiring privately must check references themselves.

title: Hospice care in New York: who qualifies, costs and choosing one
seoTitle: Hospice Care in New York: A Family Guide
seoDesc: Who qualifies for hospice under Medicare in New York, what it covers and costs, home vs inpatient care, palliative care, MOLST, and how to choose a hospice.
dek: What the Medicare hospice benefit covers, what it costs, where care happens and how to check a New York hospice before you call it.
keyFacts: Medicare hospice needs a doctor's certification of a life expectancy of six months or less.
Benefit periods: two of 90 days, then unlimited 60-day periods, with recertification.
Covered hospice care costs $0. Drugs for pain and symptoms cost up to $5 per prescription.
Respite stays for the caregiver last up to 5 days at a time.
NY DOH Home Health Hotline for hospice complaints: 1-800-628-5972.
body:
Hospice is comfort care for someone with a terminal illness, and Medicare pays for nearly all of it once a doctor certifies a life expectancy of six months or less. Hospice is usually given at home, with a team that visits on a schedule and a nurse you can call at any hour.

Ask about it early. Hospice can help for many months, and your parent can leave it at any time. This guide covers who qualifies, what Medicare covers and charges, where care happens, how hospice differs from palliative care and how to check a hospice before you choose one.

Who qualifies for hospice under Medicare?

Your mom or dad qualifies for the Medicare hospice benefit if all of these are true.

  • They have Medicare Part A.
  • The hospice doctor and their regular doctor (if they have one) certify they are terminally ill, with a life expectancy of six months or less if the illness runs its normal course.
  • They accept comfort care instead of treatment meant to cure the illness.
  • They sign a statement choosing hospice.

Hospice comes in benefit periods. There are two 90-day periods, then an unlimited number of 60-day periods. After the first six months, a hospice doctor or nurse practitioner meets with your parent face to face and the hospice must recertify that they are still terminally ill. So someone who lives longer than six months can keep getting hospice as long as they still qualify.

Your parent can switch hospice providers once in each benefit period. They also have the right to stop hospice at any time, for example to try a new treatment, and can go back to hospice later if they qualify. People in a Medicare Advantage plan can get hospice too. Original Medicare pays for the hospice care related to the terminal illness.

Hospice is a choice your parent can change. Signing up does not lock anyone in.

What does Medicare hospice cover, and what doesn't it?

Medicare says the hospice benefit should cover everything your parent needs for the terminal illness and related conditions. The hospice team writes a plan of care and arranges the services.

CoveredNot covered
Nursing visits and a doctor overseeing careTreatment meant to cure the terminal illness
Hospice aide and homemaker servicesDrugs meant to cure the illness, as opposed to easing pain and symptoms
Social worker services and grief counseling for the familyCare from providers the hospice did not arrange
Medical equipment such as wheelchairs and walkers, and suppliesRoom and board at home, in a nursing home or in a hospice residence
Drugs for pain and symptom controlHospital, emergency room or ambulance care the hospice did not arrange, unless unrelated to the terminal illness
Short-term inpatient care and respite stays the hospice arranges

Health problems that have nothing to do with the terminal illness are still covered by Original Medicare, with the usual deductibles and coinsurance. The DOH hospice services page lists other services New York hospices may offer, such as pastoral care, bereavement support for up to one year after a death, therapy and nutrition counseling.

What does hospice cost?

For most families, very little. Here is what Medicare lists on its hospice coverage page.

ItemWhat your parent pays
Covered hospice care from a Medicare-approved hospice$0
Outpatient drugs for pain and symptom controlUp to $5 per prescription
Inpatient respite care5% of the Medicare-approved amount, capped at the Part A inpatient deductible ($1,776 in 2027)
Room and board in a nursing home or residenceNot covered by Medicare hospice

Room and board is the one big cost families miss. If your dad lives in a nursing home and goes on hospice, Medicare pays for the hospice care but not his daily room charge. Ask the nursing home and the hospice how that charge will be paid, whether by savings, long-term care insurance or Medicaid. Our Medicaid guide explains the rules.

Where does hospice care happen, at home or inpatient?

Hospice is usually given at home. "Home" can also mean a nursing home or assisted living residence where your parent already lives. The hospice team visits on a schedule, and a nurse can be reached by phone at any hour. Family members or paid aides do most of the day-to-day care between visits, and the team shows you how.

Some situations call for care somewhere else.

  • Short-term inpatient care. When pain or other symptoms cannot be controlled at home, the hospice can arrange a stay in a hospice inpatient unit, a hospital or a skilled nursing facility.
  • Respite care. If the family caregiver needs a break, the hospice can arrange a stay of up to 5 days at a time in an inpatient facility, hospital or nursing home.
  • Hospice residence. Some New York hospices run a residence, a home-like setting for 3 to 16 hospice patients who cannot stay at home. Medicare hospice does not pay room and board there, so ask what it costs. Use "Search by Service" on the state profiles site to find one.

If your mom is being discharged from a hospital in Manhattan or Rochester and wants to die at home, ask the hospital to call hospices before discharge. Ask each one how quickly it can bring in a hospital bed and supplies.

How is hospice different from palliative care?

Palliative care eases pain, stress and symptoms at any stage of a serious illness, and your parent can get it alongside treatment meant to cure. Hospice is a type of palliative care for people who are terminally ill and have stopped curative treatment.

New York's Palliative Care Information Act requires attending doctors and nurse practitioners to offer patients with a terminal illness information and counseling about palliative care and end-of-life options. The law applies when the practitioner reasonably expects death within six months. If no one has raised it, you can ask. A good question is "Would hospice or palliative care help my dad right now?"

New York's Medical Aid in Dying law (Public Health Law Article 28-F) took effect on August 5, 2026. It lets terminally ill New York residents with less than six months to live request medication to end their life. A doctor must find that the patient has decision-making capacity, and a mental health evaluation is required. The patient must take the medication themselves. There is a 5-day wait between writing the prescription and filling it. The doctor must also explain other options, including palliative care and hospice. It is a separate law, not part of the Medicare hospice benefit. Read the DOH Medical Aid in Dying page and talk with your parent's doctor if it comes up.

How does MOLST fit with hospice?

MOLST (Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment) is a New York medical order form, DOH-5003, that records decisions about CPR, breathing machines, feeding tubes and hospital transfer. It is meant for people with serious illness, including those who might die within the next year, so ask the hospice team about one if your parent does not have it yet.

A health care proxy names who decides if your parent cannot. MOLST turns those choices into doctor's orders. Hospitals, hospices, nursing homes and emergency crews must follow it, including at home. DOH says to keep it at home on the refrigerator, by the phone in the kitchen or at the bedside. The doctor, nurse practitioner or physician assistant must review it at least every 90 days and after any big change. Photocopies and faxes of a signed form are valid. See our full guide to health care proxies, living wills and MOLST.

How do I check and choose a hospice in New York?

Use two sources, then interview two or three hospices that serve your parent's county.

  1. Search Care Compare. On Medicare Care Compare, choose hospice care and enter a ZIP code. You will see results from the CAHPS Hospice Survey, answered by family members who cared for a patient who died in hospice. It covers communication with family, getting timely help, treating the patient with respect, emotional and spiritual support, help for pain and symptoms, and training the family.
  2. Check the state profile. The NYS Hospice Profiles site lists every licensed hospice, the counties it is approved to serve, its services, DOH inspection results and any enforcement actions.
  3. Call and ask questions. Use the list below.
  4. Ask the doctor to refer. The hospice needs the doctor's certification. Your parent's doctor or the hospital discharge planner can send the referral.

Questions to ask each hospice:

  • How soon can a nurse come for the first visit after we call?
  • How often will the nurse and aide visit each week? Who answers the phone at 2 a.m., and how fast can a nurse come?
  • Do you offer continuous care at home during a crisis? Where do patients go for inpatient care or respite?
  • Do you have a hospice residence? What does room and board cost there?
  • What equipment and drugs do you provide, and what will we pay?
  • What grief support do you offer the family afterward, and for how long?

Before the first visit, confirm on the state profiles site that the hospice is licensed for your parent's county. If you have a problem with a hospice, call the DOH Home Health Hotline at 1-800-628-5972. It takes calls 24 hours a day, and staff answer weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. You can also email HomeHospiceCCIP@health.ny.gov.

Related guides: support for family caregivers in New York and how to read nursing home ratings.

faq.q: How do I get hospice for my mom at home in Queens?
faq.a: Ask her doctor whether she qualifies, then search Medicare Care Compare and the NYS Hospice Profiles site for hospices approved to serve Queens. Call two or three, ask about visit frequency and night coverage, and have her doctor send the referral. Medicare pays for covered hospice care at $0.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for my dad's nursing home room in Westchester if he goes on hospice?
faq.a: No. Medicare hospice pays for the hospice care, drugs for pain and symptoms and equipment, but not room and board in a nursing home. That charge is paid by savings, long-term care insurance or Medicaid if he qualifies.

faq.q: What happens if my parent lives longer than six months on hospice?
faq.a: Hospice can continue. After two 90-day periods, Medicare allows an unlimited number of 60-day periods. A hospice doctor or nurse practitioner meets with your parent and the hospice recertifies that they are still terminally ill.

faq.q: Can my parent leave hospice?
faq.a: Yes. Medicare says a person always has the right to stop hospice at any time, for example to try a new treatment. They can go back to hospice later if they still qualify.

faq.q: What is the difference between hospice and palliative care?
faq.a: Palliative care relieves symptoms at any stage of a serious illness and can be given alongside curative treatment. Hospice is palliative care for people who are terminally ill and have chosen comfort care instead of a cure.

faq.q: Who do I call with a complaint about a hospice in New York?
faq.a: Call the Department of Health Home Health Hotline at 1-800-628-5972, which takes calls 24 hours a day, or email HomeHospiceCCIP@health.ny.gov. Staff answer the phone weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m.

title: Managed long term care in New York: MLTC, NYIA and plan choice
seoTitle: Medicaid MLTC in NY: who must enroll and how to choose
seoDesc: Who must join a Medicaid managed long term care plan in NY, how the NYIA assessment works, MLTC vs MAP vs PACE, what plans cover and when you can switch.
dek: If your parent has Medicare and Medicaid and needs ongoing help at home, a managed long term care plan is usually how that help arrives. Here is how the assessment, plan choice and switching rules work in New York.
keyFacts: MLTC enrollment is mandatory for dual eligible New Yorkers 21 and older who need community long-term care for more than 120 days and meet the minimum needs test.
The New York Independent Assessor decides eligibility. Call 855-222-8350 (TTY 1-888-329-1541).
The three plan types are MLTC partial capitation, Medicaid Advantage Plus (MAP) and PACE.
Partial capitation plans have a 90-day grace period, then a 9-month lock-in before you can switch without good cause.
New York Medicaid Choice handles enrollment: 1-888-401-6582. ICAN gives free help: 1-844-614-8800.
body:
Medicaid managed long term care (MLTC) is the Medicaid system New York uses to arrange long-term help at home, such as home care aides, CDPAP and adult day health care. If your parent has both Medicare and Medicaid, is 21 or older and needs that kind of help for more than 120 days, they generally must join an MLTC plan to keep getting it.

The process has several steps: a state assessment, choosing a plan, enrolling through New York Medicaid Choice and then working with a plan care manager. This guide explains each one, the three types of plans and the rules for switching.

Who must enroll in managed long term care?

The New York State Department of Health (DOH) says enrollment in an MLTC partial capitation plan is mandatory for people who meet all of these:

  • Have both Medicare and Medicaid (called "dual eligible")
  • Are 21 or older
  • Need community based long term services and supports for more than 120 days
  • Meet the minimum needs requirement (below)
  • Live in New York State

Dual eligible people aged 18 to 20, and people 18 and older who have Medicaid but not Medicare, can join voluntarily if they meet the same needs rules.

The minimum needs requirement, from Public Health Law section 4403-f, is one of these:

  • Needs at least limited help with physical movement for more than two activities of daily living (such as bathing, dressing, toileting or moving from bed to chair), or
  • Has a dementia or Alzheimer's diagnosis and needs at least supervision with more than one activity of daily living

DOH notes that the older (legacy) criteria apply to people assessed before September 1, 2025. DOH also says needing only housekeeping and shopping help does not meet the need for this level of care. If that is all your parent needs, look at the EISEP program through the county Office for the Aging instead.

Your parent must also already have Medicaid. That is decided by HRA in New York City or the county Department of Social Services elsewhere. Start with our Medicaid guide if they don't.

How does the New York Independent Assessor (NYIA) process work?

Before anyone can join an MLTC plan or start Medicaid personal care or CDPAP, the New York Independent Assessor Program (NYIAP) does the initial assessment. DOH contracted with Maximus Health Services to run it starting May 2022.

  1. Call NYIA. Your parent, or an authorized representative on file with NYIA, calls 855-222-8350 (TTY 1-888-329-1541) to schedule.
  2. Community Health Assessment. A registered nurse does a full assessment. DOH says most take two to three hours. Your parent can choose in person or by video.
  3. Clinical appointment. A clinician from the Independent Practitioner Panel examines your parent. DOH says this takes up to one hour, in person or by video, and that a practitioner order is completed for all initial NYIA assessments.
  4. Independent Review Panel, if needed. When a proposed plan of care is for more than 12 hours a day on average, a separate panel reviews it.
  5. Choose and enroll in a plan. Once NYIA finds your parent eligible, call New York Medicaid Choice (below) to pick an MLTC plan.
  6. Plan of care. The plan's care manager works with your parent to set the services and hours.

DOH says the Community Health Assessment can stay valid for up to 12 months, with a new one after a change in medical condition, after leaving institutional care or on request. NYIA also does reassessments for personal care and CDPAP, and a physician order is needed before each reassessment. If your parent is not yet getting services and has an urgent change in condition, DOH says to contact the local social services district or their Medicaid managed care plan, which can help schedule an assessment quickly.

Be there for the nurse's assessment. A family member who knows the hard days can describe them.

What are the three types of MLTC plans?

Plan typeAgeCoverage neededWhat the plan handles
MLTC partial capitation ("MLTC Medicaid Plan")18+MedicaidLong-term care and related services, including home care and up to three months of long-term nursing home care. Medicare and regular Medicaid cover doctors, hospitals and drugs.
Medicaid Advantage Plus (MAP)18+Medicaid and Medicare Parts A and BAll Medicare, Medicaid, long-term care and drug benefits under one organization, through the plan's aligned Medicare Advantage Dual Special Needs Plan
PACE55+Medicaid, Medicare or private payAll medically necessary primary, acute and long-term care, through one team. Must need nursing home level care.

MAP and PACE fold everything into one plan, which can mean fewer hand-offs between Medicare and Medicaid. A partial capitation plan leaves your parent's Medicare coverage and doctors as they are. For PACE details and the counties where it runs, see our PACE guide.

What does an MLTC plan cover?

DOH lists these services as covered by MLTC plans when medically necessary:

  • Care management
  • Home care, including nursing, home health aides and therapy
  • Personal care
  • Consumer Directed Personal Assistance Services (see our CDPAP guide)
  • Adult day health care (see our adult day care guide)
  • Nursing home care (limited to three months of long-term stay in partial plans)
  • Medical equipment and supplies, and a personal emergency response system
  • Non-emergency transportation
  • Dental, podiatry, eye care and eyeglasses, audiology and hearing aids
  • Therapies outside the home, respiratory therapy, nutrition and private duty nursing
  • Home-delivered or congregate meals, social day care and social and environmental supports

In a partial capitation plan, DOH lists hospital care, doctor visits, lab work, prescription drugs and the Assisted Living Program as outside the plan. Those are billed to Medicare or regular Medicaid. MAP covers mental health and substance use services as of January 1, 2023.

About nursing home stays

DOH says MLTC Medicaid (partial capitation) plans cover only three months of long-term nursing home care. If a long-term stay goes past three months, New York Medicaid Choice sends a letter saying when your parent will leave the plan. DOH says the plans do cover temporary nursing home stays.

How do I choose and enroll in a plan?

Enrollment goes through New York Medicaid Choice (NYMC), the state's enrollment broker, at 1-888-401-6582 (TTY 1-888-329-1541). Its site and DOH list hours of 8:30 a.m. to 8 p.m. Monday through Friday and 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Saturday. You can also compare plans at nymedicaidchoice.com.

Not every plan serves every county. DOH's MLTC plan directory shows the plans approved in each county. DOH also publishes consumer quality guides that rate plans and include members' opinions.

Questions worth asking each plan:

  • Does my parent's current home care agency or adult day program contract with you?
  • If my parent uses CDPAP, how do you handle it?
  • How fast do you authorize a change in hours after a hospital stay?
  • How do I reach the care manager, and how often will they check in?
  • For MAP: are my parent's doctors and pharmacy in the Medicare plan network?

DOH suggests checking whether your parent's doctor is in the plan and whether the plan offers any special services they need.

Can my parent switch MLTC plans?

Yes, within limits. For partial capitation plans, DOH's lock-in rules (MLTC Policy 21.04) apply to enrollments effective December 1, 2020 or later:

PeriodWhat your parent can do
First 90 days after enrolling (grace period)Transfer to another partial capitation plan for any reason
Next 9 months (lock-in)Transfer only with good cause
After lock-in endsTransfer at any time

Each new enrollment or transfer restarts the clock. Under DOH's policy, good cause includes the plan failing to provide appropriate care under the plan of care, moving out of the service area, being enrolled without consent, the current home care provider not contracting with the plan, the plan and member agreeing a move is in the member's interest, or DOH finding the plan broke its contract. To transfer, call New York Medicaid Choice.

The lock-in does not apply to MAP or PACE, to transfers into those plans, or to people who joined voluntarily (dual eligible people aged 18 to 20 and people without Medicare).

Where can I get free help with an MLTC problem?

The Independent Consumer Advocacy Network (ICAN), a group of nonprofit advocacy organizations, helps people in MLTC, MAP and PACE plans and people thinking about joining one. DOH says ICAN is independent of the Department of Health and of any health plan, and its help is free and confidential. ICAN can answer questions, fix problems with plans and providers, and help you file a complaint or appeal. Family members and representatives can call.

  • ICAN: 1-844-614-8800 (TTY relay 711), 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. per DOH, icannys.org
  • New York Medicaid Choice: 1-888-401-6582
  • DOH managed long term care email: MLTCinfo@health.ny.gov
  • NY Connects: 1-800-342-9871

If your parent's needs grow beyond what home care can safely provide, our guides to assisted living, memory care and nursing homes can help with next steps.

faq.q: How do I get my mom home care through Medicaid in the Bronx?
faq.a: She needs Medicaid through HRA first. Then call the New York Independent Assessor at 855-222-8350 (TTY 1-888-329-1541) to schedule the nurse assessment and clinical appointment. If she qualifies and has Medicare too, she enrolls in a plan through New York Medicaid Choice at 1-888-401-6582, and the plan's care manager sets her home care plan.

faq.q: Can my dad in Orange County switch his MLTC plan if the aide keeps missing shifts?
faq.a: In the first 90 days after enrolling he can switch for any reason. During the following nine-month lock-in he needs good cause, and a plan failing to provide appropriate care under the plan of care counts. Call New York Medicaid Choice at 1-888-401-6582, and ICAN at 1-844-614-8800 can help.

faq.q: Who has to join a managed long term care plan in New York?
faq.a: DOH says enrollment in an MLTC partial capitation plan is mandatory for people with both Medicare and Medicaid, age 21 or older, who need community based long-term services for more than 120 days, meet the minimum needs test and live in New York State.

faq.q: What is the difference between MLTC, MAP and PACE?
faq.a: An MLTC partial capitation plan covers long-term care like home care, while Medicare and regular Medicaid cover doctors, hospitals and drugs. Medicaid Advantage Plus puts all Medicare, Medicaid, long-term care and drug benefits under one organization. PACE, for people 55 and older, covers primary, acute and long-term care through one team.

faq.q: Does an MLTC plan cover CDPAP?
faq.a: Yes. DOH lists Consumer Directed Personal Assistance Services among the services MLTC plans cover when medically necessary. The plan authorizes the hours.

faq.q: What happens to the MLTC plan if my parent moves into a nursing home?
faq.a: DOH says MLTC partial capitation plans cover only three months of long-term nursing home care. If the stay goes past three months, New York Medicaid Choice sends a letter saying when your parent will leave the plan.
