title: Medicare costs in 2027 for New Yorkers
seoTitle: Medicare Costs 2027 in New York: Premiums and IRMAA
seoDesc: 2027 Medicare costs for New Yorkers: $209.40 Part B premium, $292 deductible, $1,776 Part A deductible, IRMAA brackets, the $2,400 Part D cap, and NY help.
dek: Every main 2027 Medicare premium, deductible and coinsurance figure from CMS, in plain English, plus the New York programs (Medicare Savings Program, Extra Help and EPIC) that can lower the bill.
keyFacts: 2027 Part B premium is $209.40 a month (up from $202.90). Part B deductible is $292.
Part A hospital deductible is $1,776 per benefit period in 2027.
IRMAA starts above $112,000 single or $224,000 joint income.
Part D out-of-pocket cap for covered drugs is $2,400 in 2027.
New York's Medicare Savings Program has no resource test. Free help from HIICAP: 1-800-701-0501.
body:
In 2027 most New Yorkers on Medicare pay a standard Part B premium of $209.40 a month and a Part B deductible of $292 for the year. A hospital stay starts with a $1,776 Part A deductible, and Part D drug plans cap your out-of-pocket drug costs at $2,400.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) released these numbers on November 17, 2026. They take effect January 1, 2027. Below you will find every main figure, what it means for your mom or dad, and the New York programs that can bring the bill down. If money is tight, the section on lowering costs may matter most.

What does Medicare Part B cost in 2027?

Part B is the part of Medicare that pays for doctor visits, outpatient care, lab tests and medical equipment. Almost everyone pays a monthly premium for it.

Part B item20262027
Standard monthly premium$202.90$209.40
Yearly deductible$283$292

The premium goes up $6.50 a month. CMS says the increase is mainly due to projected growth in health care spending. After your parent meets the $292 deductible, they usually pay 20% of the cost for each Medicare-covered service or item, according to Medicare.gov. Original Medicare has no yearly limit on what you pay out of pocket unless you have supplemental coverage.

Those leftover costs are a big reason many New Yorkers buy a Medigap policy or join a Medicare Advantage plan. Medicare Advantage plans have a yearly limit on out-of-pocket costs, which Original Medicare lacks. Our guide to Medigap in New York explains the state's buyer protections, which go further than federal rules.

Who pays more than the standard premium?

People with higher incomes pay an extra charge called the Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount (IRMAA). Social Security sets it using the most recent federal tax return the IRS sends. For 2026 premiums, Social Security says that was generally the return for tax year 2024, so the income year usually runs two years behind the premium year.

2027 income (single)2027 income (married filing jointly)Part B monthly premiumPart D extra each month
$112,000 or less$224,000 or less$209.40$0
Over $112,000 up to $141,000Over $224,000 up to $282,000$293.10$15.40
Over $141,000 up to $177,000Over $282,000 up to $354,000$418.80$39.70
Over $177,000 up to $212,000Over $354,000 up to $424,000$544.40$64.00
Over $212,000 and under $500,000Over $424,000 and under $750,000$670.00$88.30
$500,000 or more$750,000 or more$711.80$96.40

The Part D amount is added on top of whatever the drug plan itself charges. Married people who file separately and lived with their spouse face a steeper scale. They pay $209.40 at $112,000 or less, $670.00 above $112,000 and under $388,000, and $711.80 at $388,000 or more.

Can my parent ask to lower IRMAA?

Yes, if a life-changing event cut their income. Social Security lists marriage, divorce, the death of a spouse, loss of income (such as retiring) and an employer settlement payment. Your parent files form SSA-44 with proof, online, by mail or fax, or by calling 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778). This comes up a lot in the first year or two after retirement, when last year's paycheck no longer reflects real income.

What does Part A cost for a hospital or nursing home stay?

Part A covers inpatient hospital care, care in a skilled nursing facility after a qualifying hospital stay, hospice and some home health care. CMS says about 99% of people on Medicare pay no Part A premium, because they or a spouse worked long enough. The costs show up when someone is admitted.

Part A item20262027
Hospital deductible (covers your share of days 1 to 60 in a benefit period)$1,736$1,776
Hospital coinsurance, days 61 to 90$434 a day$444 a day
Lifetime reserve days$868 a day$888 a day
Skilled nursing facility coinsurance, days 21 to 100$217 a day$222 a day

The deductible applies to each benefit period, and one year can hold more than one. So a parent who goes into a Rochester hospital in March and again in October can owe it twice. Rehab costs climb quickly after day 20 in a skilled nursing facility. If your dad is heading from a hospital to short-term rehab, ask the discharge planner what his coverage will pay and check facilities with our guide to nursing home ratings in New York.

What if my parent does not have 40 quarters of work?

Premium-free Part A generally requires 40 quarters (about 10 years) of work that paid Medicare taxes, by your parent or a spouse. People with fewer quarters can buy Part A.

Work history2026 Part A premium2027 Part A premium
40 or more quarters$0$0
30 to 39 quarters$311 a month$328 a month
Fewer than 30 quarters$565 a month$597 a month

This often affects people who came to New York later in life or spent years caring for family at home. Check a spouse's record too, since a spouse's work can count. If money is tight, New York's Qualified Medicare Beneficiary program (described below) can pay the Part A premium for people who lack enough work history.

What will prescriptions cost under Part D in 2027?

Part D is drug coverage sold by private plans, either alone or inside a Medicare Advantage plan. Each plan sets its own premium and drug list, but federal rules set the outer limits.

Part D limit20262027
Highest deductible a plan can charge$615$700
Yearly cap on out-of-pocket costs for covered drugs$2,100$2,400
National base beneficiary premium (used to figure late penalties)$38.99$41.33

Medicare.gov says the $2,400 cap counts your parent's deductible, their out-of-pocket spending on covered drugs, and certain payments made on their behalf, such as through Extra Help. Once that total reaches $2,400, they pay $0 for each covered drug for the rest of 2027. The plan's monthly premium is a separate cost.

The $2,400 cap is the ceiling, and help programs can bring the floor much lower.

Plans change their premiums and drug lists every year. Open enrollment for 2027 runs through December 7, 2026. See our open enrollment guide for how to compare plans.

How can New Yorkers lower their Medicare costs?

Three New York programs do most of the work.

Medicare Savings Program (MSP)

The MSP pays Medicare costs for people with modest incomes. New York has no resource test for the MSP, so savings, a house or a car do not count against your parent. There are two levels.

2026 New York MSP levelWhat it paysMonthly income, singleMonthly income, couple
Qualified Medicare Beneficiary (QMB), 138% of povertyPart B premium, Part A premium if owed, plus Medicare deductibles and coinsuranceUp to $1,836Up to $2,489
Qualifying Individual (QI), over 138% up to 186% of povertyPart B premiumUp to $2,474Up to $3,355

These are the state's 2026 limits. They usually rise each year when federal poverty levels update, so apply even if your parent is a little over. Say your mom lives alone in Syracuse and her income is about $2,200 a month. She may fall within the QI level, and the program would pay her $209.40 Part B premium. That is $2,512.80 back in her pocket over 2027. The county decides how income is counted, so let them do the math.

The application is form DOH-4328, and approval brings Extra Help automatically. In New York City, you can get help at a Human Resources Administration (HRA) Medicaid office (HRA Helpline 1-888-692-6113). Everywhere else, contact your county Department of Social Services. Read more in our Medicare Savings Program guide.

Extra Help with drug costs

Extra Help is the federal program that lowers Part D costs. Anyone enrolled in an MSP, full Medicaid or Supplemental Security Income (SSI) gets it automatically. In 2027, people with Extra Help pay no more than $5.80 for each generic drug and $14.40 for each brand-name drug, according to Medicare.gov. For 2026, Medicare.gov lists income limits of $23,940 for a single person and $32,460 for a married couple, with resource limits of $18,090 and $36,100. Others apply through Social Security at 1-800-772-1213. See our Extra Help guide.

EPIC drug coverage

Elderly Pharmaceutical Insurance Coverage (EPIC) is New York State's drug program for residents 65 and older. It works as secondary coverage on top of a Part D plan, helping after the Part D deductible. The income limits are far higher than Extra Help.

  • Fee Plan. Income up to $20,000 single or $26,000 married.
  • Deductible Plan. Income from $20,001 to $75,000 single, or $26,001 to $100,000 married.
  • Help with Part D premiums. Available up to $23,000 single or $29,000 married.

Call EPIC at 1-800-332-3742 or read our EPIC guide.

  1. Gather the numbers. Get your parent's monthly Social Security, pension and other income, plus their Medicare card and current drug list.
  2. Call HIICAP for a free screening. New York's Health Insurance Information Counseling and Assistance Program (HIICAP) can check MSP, Extra Help and EPIC at once. Call 1-800-701-0501, Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
  3. Apply for the MSP first. Approval brings Extra Help automatically, which lowers drug costs too.
  4. Add EPIC. If your parent is 65 or older, an EPIC application can cover gaps that remain.
  5. Check the next Social Security statement. Once the MSP starts paying Part B, the $209.40 should stop coming out of the check.

Where can my family get free help with Medicare costs?

HIICAP counselors are based in local offices for the aging across the state. When you call 1-800-701-0501, you say your county and get routed to the local program. The New York State Office for the Aging (NYSOFA) says HIICAP can screen for the MSP, and that people who enroll can save up to an estimated $8,400 a year.

  • New York City. Call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 (212-AGING-NYC) or HIICAP NYC at 212-341-3978. NYC Aging says HIICAP counselors are available throughout the city.
  • Rest of the state. The statewide HIICAP line routes you to your county's program. NY Connects (1-800-342-9871) offers free information on long-term services and supports. Find your county on our NY Connects guide.
  • Medicare itself. 1-800-633-4227 (1-800-MEDICARE), TTY 1-877-486-2048.
Check the first 2027 payment

Look at your parent's first Social Security payment or benefit notice for 2027. The standard Part B amount is $209.40, so a higher figure means IRMAA applies. If it looks wrong, call Social Security rather than paying it all year. Our Social Security 2027 guide covers the raise.

faq.q: How much is the Medicare Part B premium in 2027?
faq.a: The standard Part B premium is $209.40 a month in 2027, up from $202.90 in 2026. The yearly Part B deductible is $292. People with income above $112,000 (single) or $224,000 (joint) pay more under IRMAA.

faq.q: How do I get help paying my mom's Medicare premium in Queens?
faq.a: Apply for New York's Medicare Savings Program, which has no resource test. In New York City you can get help at an HRA Medicaid office (HRA Helpline 1-888-692-6113). For free help with the form, call HIICAP NYC at 212-341-3978 or Aging Connect at 212-244-6469.

faq.q: What is the Part A deductible for 2027?
faq.a: The Part A inpatient hospital deductible is $1,776 per benefit period in 2027. It covers your share of the first 60 days. Days 61 to 90 cost $444 a day, and skilled nursing days 21 to 100 cost $222 a day.

faq.q: What is the most my dad in Albany will pay for prescriptions in 2027?
faq.a: With a Part D plan, his out-of-pocket costs for covered drugs are capped at $2,400 for 2027. After that he pays $0 for covered drugs for the rest of the year, though his plan premium is a separate cost. If his income is modest, Extra Help or New York's EPIC program can lower costs further. HIICAP (1-800-701-0501) can check both for free.

faq.q: What does Part A cost if you do not have 40 work quarters?
faq.a: In 2027 Part A costs $328 a month with 30 to 39 quarters of work and $597 a month with fewer than 30. A spouse's work record can count. New York's QMB program can pay the Part A premium for people who qualify by income.

faq.q: Can I appeal a high IRMAA charge?
faq.a: Yes. If income dropped because of retirement, marriage, divorce, a spouse's death or similar events, file form SSA-44 with Social Security. You can submit it online, by mail or fax, or call 1-800-772-1213.

title: Medicare open enrollment and changing plans in New York
seoTitle: Medicare Open Enrollment in New York: Dates and Help
seoDesc: Medicare open enrollment runs Oct 15 to Dec 7. Learn the Jan 1 to Mar 31 Advantage window, special enrollment periods, free HIICAP help and plan scams in NY.
dek: The dates that matter, what you can change in each window, how to compare plans on Medicare.gov, and where New York families get free help before December 7.
keyFacts: Annual Open Enrollment runs October 15 to December 7. Changes start January 1.
Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment runs January 1 to March 31, with one change allowed.
New York Medigap insurers must accept applicants any time of year.
Free counseling from HIICAP: 1-800-701-0501, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
NYSOFA says plans may not call, email or visit your home to market a plan.
body:
Medicare open enrollment runs from October 15 to December 7 every year, and the choices you make take effect January 1. If your parent is in a Medicare Advantage plan, a second window from January 1 to March 31 allows one more change.

Right now, in late November 2026, the window for 2027 coverage is still open until December 7. This guide covers what you can change and when, how to compare plans on Medicare.gov, where to get free counseling in New York, and how to spot the calls and mailers that are really sales pitches.

What can I change between October 15 and December 7?

During the annual Open Enrollment Period, anyone with Medicare can make these moves.

  • Switch from Original Medicare to a Medicare Advantage plan, or the other way around.
  • Switch from one Medicare Advantage plan to another.
  • Join, switch or drop a stand-alone Part D drug plan.

The last choice you make before December 7 is the one that counts, and it starts January 1. If your parent does nothing, they usually stay in the same plan. That plan may have new premiums, a new drug list or a new set of doctors for 2027, so read the Annual Notice of Change the plan mailed in the fall.

Enrollment windowDatesChanges start
Annual Open EnrollmentOctober 15 to December 7January 1
Medicare Advantage Open EnrollmentJanuary 1 to March 31First of the month after the plan gets your request

A few 2027 numbers help when you compare. The standard Part B premium is $209.40 a month. Part D plans can charge a deductible of no more than $700, and out-of-pocket costs for covered drugs are capped at $2,400 for the year. Our 2027 Medicare costs guide has every figure.

What is the Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period?

From January 1 to March 31, people already in a Medicare Advantage plan get one chance to change. New enrollees who joined Medicare Advantage when they first got Medicare also get this chance during their first three months with Parts A and B.

  • Your parent can switch to a different Medicare Advantage plan.
  • Or they can drop Medicare Advantage, return to Original Medicare and join a stand-alone Part D plan.

Only one change is allowed in this window. It cannot be used to move from Original Medicare into Medicare Advantage, or to switch Part D plans while on Original Medicare.

Why New York makes the January window more useful

In most states, someone who leaves Medicare Advantage may struggle to buy a Medigap policy because insurers can check their health. New York law requires Medigap insurers to accept applications from Medicare enrollees at any time of year, and they cannot charge more based on health. A policy may still have a waiting period of up to six months before pre-existing conditions are covered. Our Medigap in New York guide explains how that wait gets shortened.

Can my parent change plans at other times of year?

Yes, if a Special Enrollment Period applies. These are the ones New York families run into most.

  • Moving. A move out of the plan's service area opens a window. If you tell the plan before the move, it starts the month before and runs two full months after. A move within the area to a place with new plan options also counts.
  • Moving into or out of a nursing home. Your parent can join, switch or drop coverage while living in a nursing home or similar institution and for two full months after the month they move out.
  • Losing job-based coverage. When employer or union coverage ends, the chance to join lasts two full months after the month it ends.
  • Losing Medicaid. Three full months from the later of the date eligibility ends or the date you are notified.
  • Medicaid or Extra Help. People with these programs get extra chances to change during the year. HIICAP can tell you which ones apply.
  • EPIC. Members of a State Pharmaceutical Assistance Program, which in New York means EPIC, can join a Part D plan once each calendar year outside open enrollment.
  • A 5-star plan. You can switch into a plan rated 5 stars once, between December 8 and November 30.

Write down the date of the move, discharge or coverage loss. The clock starts from it, and two months goes fast after a hospital stay.

How do I compare plans on Medicare.gov?

The Medicare Plan Finder shows every plan sold in your parent's ZIP code, with estimated yearly costs for their own drugs. It is Medicare's own tool.

  1. Collect what you need. Your parent's Medicare card, ZIP code, every prescription with dose and how often it is filled, and the pharmacies they use.
  2. Open Plan Finder. Go to Medicare.gov/plan-compare and enter your parent's ZIP code.
  3. Enter drugs and pharmacies. Pick one or two pharmacies. Prices can differ a lot between a chain in Yonkers and a local pharmacy in Elmira.
  4. Sort by total estimated cost. Look past the premium. The yearly total adds premiums and expected drug costs together.
  5. Check the doctors. For Medicare Advantage plans, call each doctor's office and ask whether they will be in that plan's network for 2027. Online directories are not always current.
  6. Enroll and save proof. Enroll through Plan Finder or by calling 1-800-633-4227. Write down the confirmation number and the date.

Comparing for two parents? Run each one separately. Drug lists differ, so the right plan for your mom may be wrong for your dad.

Where can we get free help in New York?

New York's free Medicare counseling program is HIICAP, the Health Insurance Information, Counseling and Assistance Program. NYSOFA says it helps about 220,000 New Yorkers a year with Medicare decisions.

  • Statewide helpline. 1-800-701-0501, Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Say your county and the call goes to your local program.
  • New York City. HIICAP NYC at 212-341-3978, or Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 (212-AGING-NYC). Counselors work across all five boroughs.
  • Outside the city. HIICAP counselors are based in local offices for the aging. The statewide line routes you by county. NY Connects (1-800-342-9871) offers free information on long-term services and supports.

The New York State Office for the Aging (NYSOFA) says more than 700 trained HIICAP counselors work across the state. They can compare Part D plans, weigh Original Medicare against Medicare Advantage, explain bills and appeals, and screen for the Medicare Savings Program and EPIC. Call well before the December 7 deadline.

One free call to a counselor can sort out a dozen glossy mailers.

How do I spot a Medicare plan scam?

NYSOFA warns that fraud risk goes up during open enrollment. It reminds families that plans are not allowed to call, email, visit the home or approach people in public to market their plan.

  • Be wary of "Medicare" callers. NYSOFA warns about people who claim to represent Medicare. A caller who asks for a Medicare number is a red flag.
  • Ignore threats. Be wary of anyone who says your parent will lose benefits unless they enroll in a certain plan today.
  • Guard the Medicare number. Treat it like a Social Security or credit card number.
  • Slow down on pressure. A real plan will still be there tomorrow, and open enrollment lasts until December 7.
  • Check before acting. If someone asks for your parent's Medicare number or personal details, hang up and call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) or HIICAP to check what is real.
If your parent already said yes on the phone

Call 1-800-MEDICARE or HIICAP right away. Ask which plan your parent is enrolled in for January 1. If it is not what they wanted, a counselor can help them pick again before December 7 or explain other options.

What mistakes should we avoid this fall?

  • Choosing by premium alone. A $0 premium plan can cost more over the year if your parent's drugs sit on a high tier.
  • Skipping the drug list check. Plans change their drug lists every year. A plan that worked in 2026 may not cover the same drug the same way in 2027.
  • Assuming the doctor is in network. Call and ask about 2027 by plan name.
  • Missing low-income help. If money is tight, check the Medicare Savings Program, Extra Help and EPIC. In New York, MSP approval brings Extra Help automatically.
  • Forgetting dual coverage. If your parent has Medicaid too, look at how plans coordinate with it. Our Medicaid guide covers the basics, and PACE may fit someone who needs nursing-home-level care at home.

faq.q: When is Medicare open enrollment for 2027 coverage?
faq.a: Open enrollment runs from October 15 to December 7, 2026, and changes start January 1, 2027. People in Medicare Advantage get one more change from January 1 to March 31, 2027.

faq.q: How do I help my dad pick a Medicare drug plan in Buffalo?
faq.a: List his drugs, doses and pharmacy, then enter them in the Medicare Plan Finder at medicare.gov and sort by total estimated cost. For a free walk-through, call HIICAP at 1-800-701-0501 and say you are in Erie County to reach the local counselors.

faq.q: Someone called my mom in Brooklyn offering a better Medicare plan. Is it real?
faq.a: Be careful. NYSOFA says plans are not allowed to call people to market a plan. Do not give out her Medicare number. Call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) or HIICAP NYC at 212-341-3978 to check her options.

faq.q: Can I leave Medicare Advantage and go back to Original Medicare?
faq.a: Yes, during open enrollment (October 15 to December 7) or the Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period (January 1 to March 31). In New York, Medigap insurers must accept you any time, though a waiting period of up to six months for pre-existing conditions may apply.

faq.q: What is HIICAP?
faq.a: HIICAP is New York's free Medicare counseling program, with counselors based in local offices for the aging. Call 1-800-701-0501, Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., and say your county.

faq.q: Can I change plans if I move or go into a nursing home?
faq.a: Yes. Moving out of your plan's area opens a Special Enrollment Period, and so does living in or leaving a nursing home. In the nursing home case, the window lasts while your parent lives there and for two full months after the month they move out.

title: Medigap in New York: buy any time, same price at any age
seoTitle: Medigap in New York: Open Enrollment and Rates
seoDesc: In New York you can buy Medigap any time and age never raises the price. Learn the plans sold, how to compare DFS rates, and Medigap vs Medicare Advantage.
dek: New York lets older adults buy a Medicare Supplement policy any month of the year at a community-rated price. Here is how it works, what is sold and how to compare.
keyFacts: New York Medigap insurers must accept Medicare enrollees any time of year.
Premiums are community rated, without regard to age, sex, health or tobacco use.
A pre-existing condition wait of up to 6 months may apply, shortened by prior coverage.
Plans C, F and F+ are only for people first eligible for Medicare before 2020.
Compare 2027 premiums in the DFS comparison tables. Free help from HIICAP: 1-800-701-0501.
body:
In New York, your parent can buy a Medigap policy any time of year, and insurers cannot turn them down or charge more because of their health. Premiums are also community rated, so a 66-year-old and an 86-year-old in the same region pay the same price for the same plan from the same company.

Those rules go well beyond what federal law requires. This guide explains what Medigap covers, how New York's protections work, which plans are sold here, how to compare prices on the Department of Financial Services (DFS) site, and how to weigh Medigap against Medicare Advantage.

What is Medigap?

Medigap, also called Medicare Supplement Insurance, is a private policy that helps pay costs Original Medicare leaves behind, such as deductibles, coinsurance and copayments. In 2027, those gaps include a $1,776 Part A hospital deductible, a $292 Part B deductible and the 20% coinsurance owed on most Part B services. Original Medicare has no yearly limit on what you pay out of pocket unless you have supplemental coverage like Medigap.

  • Your parent needs both Part A and Part B to buy one.
  • A policy covers one person. Spouses each buy their own.
  • Medigap policies sold after 2005 do not include drug coverage. Your parent needs a separate Part D plan, and New York's EPIC program can help on top of it.
  • Medigap does not work with Medicare Advantage. Your parent picks one path or the other.
  • Standardized policies renew automatically each year, even with health problems. The insurer can only drop someone for not paying, for lying on the application, or if the company goes under.

Your parent still pays the Part B premium ($209.40 a month in 2027) on top of the Medigap premium. See the full list in our 2027 Medicare costs guide.

Can my parent buy Medigap at any time in New York?

Yes. Federal rules guarantee a Medigap sale only during a six-month window that starts the first day of the month you are 65 or older and signed up for Part B. After that, Medicare.gov says there is no federal guarantee an insurer will sell you a policy, and it may cost more because of health problems.

New York goes further. DFS says state law and regulation require any insurer writing Medigap to accept a Medicare enrollee's application at any time throughout the year. Insurers may not deny the policy or set premiums based on health status, claims history, medical conditions or whether someone is getting care. The protections apply whether your parent has Medicare because of age or disability, including end-stage renal disease.

Is there a waiting period for pre-existing conditions?

There can be. New York allows a Medigap policy to have a waiting period of up to six months before it covers pre-existing conditions. Insurers must shorten that wait by the number of days your parent had creditable coverage, as long as there was no break in coverage longer than 63 days. The DFS rate table lists each insurer's wait, and most show six months, though a few are shorter.

Timing matters here. If your mom is leaving a job-based plan or a Medicare Advantage plan, line up the Medigap start date so the gap stays under 63 days. Ask the insurer in writing how it will credit her prior coverage.

In New York, a diagnosis does not lock your parent out of Medigap.

Does age or health change the price in New York?

No. New York Insurance Law section 3231 requires Medigap policies sold in the state to be community rated, which the law defines as rating "without regard to age, sex, health status, tobacco usage or occupation." In many other states, prices climb with each birthday. Here they do not.

Prices do differ by insurer and by where your parent lives. The DFS comparison tables sort premiums into ten regions by the first three digits of the ZIP code.

DFS regionZIP codes starting with
NYC Proper100 to 104, 111 to 114
Long Island110, 115 to 119
Westchester105 to 109
Mid-Hudson124 to 127
Albany120 to 123, 128 to 129
Utica133 to 135
Watertown136
Syracuse130 to 132, 137 to 139, 148 to 149
Rochester144 to 146
Buffalo140 to 143, 147

Community rating means younger, healthy buyers often pay more than they would in an age-rated state. The tradeoff is price stability as your parent ages, and the freedom to switch later.

Which Medigap plans are sold in New York?

Medigap plans are standardized and named by letter. A Plan G from one company has the same basic benefits as a Plan G from another, so the real differences are price, service and the company's rate history. DFS lists these approved plans as of June 1, 2026.

PlansWho can buy
A, B, D, G, K, L, M, NAnyone with Part A and Part B
G+ (high deductible)Anyone with Part A and Part B
C, F and F+ (F+ is high deductible)Only people who first became eligible for Medicare before January 1, 2020

Not every insurer sells every plan in every region. A high-deductible plan has a lower premium, but your parent pays a set amount out of pocket before the policy starts paying. Ask the insurer for the 2027 deductible amount before choosing one.

How do I compare Medigap prices on the DFS website?

DFS publishes every approved insurer's monthly premiums. The newest comparison tables show premiums in effect as of January 1, 2027.

  1. Find the region. Use the first three digits of your parent's ZIP code and the table above.
  2. Use the rate look-up. Enter the ZIP code in the DFS Medicare Supplement Rate Look-up for a list of insurers and current monthly rates.
  3. Pick one or two plan letters. Compare the same letter across companies. A cheaper Plan N against a pricier Plan G is a different trade, so compare like with like first.
  4. Check the pre-existing condition wait. The DFS supplement plans page lists each insurer's wait in months.
  5. Call two or three insurers. DFS notes a listed premium may apply to part or all of a region. Confirm your parent's exact rate, the start date and any household or payment discounts.
  6. Line up drug coverage. Enroll in a Part D plan during open enrollment (through December 7) or another valid window. Medigap will not cover prescriptions.

Insurers can change premiums over time. Check the DFS tables each fall when you review your parent's Part D plan.

Can my parent switch Medigap plans or companies later?

Yes. Because New York insurers must accept Medicare enrollees any time of year, your parent can move to a different company or a different plan letter when prices or needs change. The same community-rated premium applies, and health cannot be held against them.

Say your mom in Utica has had Plan G for years and her premium keeps rising. You can look up the Utica region on the DFS tables, find a lower-priced Plan G from another insurer, and apply in any month. DFS says insurers must reduce any pre-existing condition wait by the days of prior creditable coverage, as long as there was no break longer than 63 days. Ask the new insurer to confirm how it will credit her current policy.

  • Keep the old policy until the new one starts. Get the new policy's start date in writing, then cancel the old one so there is no gap.
  • Compare the same letter. Moving from Plan G to Plan N lowers the premium but changes what your parent pays at the doctor. Ask both companies to explain the difference.
  • Ask about the wait. Confirm in writing that prior coverage will be credited.
  • Remember the 2020 rule. Someone first eligible for Medicare on or after January 1, 2020 cannot switch into Plan C, F or F+.

Should my parent choose Medigap or Medicare Advantage?

Both cover the same Medicare services. They differ in how your parent pays and which doctors they can see.

QuestionOriginal Medicare plus Medigap plus Part DMedicare Advantage
Doctors and hospitalsAny provider in the U.S. that accepts MedicareUsually a plan network, with rules for out-of-network care
Monthly costPart B premium, Medigap premium and Part D premiumPart B premium plus the plan premium, which may be $0
Costs when sickMostly covered, depending on plan letterCopays and coinsurance set by the plan
Yearly out-of-pocket limitNone in Original Medicare alone; Medigap fills most gapsYes, every plan has a yearly limit
Drug coverageSeparate Part D planUsually built in
Switching later in New YorkCan change Medigap insurers any timeCan leave in open enrollment or January 1 to March 31, then buy Medigap any time

Medigap often suits someone who sees specialists, splits time between Manhattan and Florida, or wants predictable costs. Medicare Advantage often suits someone who wants a lower monthly bill and is comfortable with a network. New York's any-time Medigap rule takes a lot of the risk out of trying Medicare Advantage first. Our open enrollment guide covers the dates.

If money is tight

Medigap premiums in New York can be high. If your parent's income is modest, check the Medicare Savings Program before buying. Its QMB level pays Medicare deductibles and coinsurance, which can make Medigap unnecessary. If your parent has full Medicaid, ask HIICAP whether Medigap makes sense at all.

Who can help us decide?

HIICAP, New York's free Medicare counseling program, answers Medigap questions. Call 1-800-701-0501, Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., and say your county. In New York City, call HIICAP NYC at 212-341-3978 or Aging Connect at 212-244-6469.

  • Bring your parent's Medicare card, current coverage, doctor list and drug list.
  • Ask the counselor to compare Medigap plus Part D with two or three Medicare Advantage plans in your parent's county.
  • If an agent is involved, ask whether they are licensed in New York and which companies they represent. A good agent will not mind the question.

faq.q: Can you buy a Medigap plan any time in New York?
faq.a: Yes. New York law requires insurers selling Medigap to accept a Medicare enrollee's application at any time of year, and they cannot deny you or charge more because of your health. A pre-existing condition waiting period of up to six months may apply.

faq.q: Does Medigap cost more as you get older in New York?
faq.a: No. New York requires Medigap to be community rated, meaning premiums are set without regard to age, sex, health status, tobacco use or occupation. Prices vary by insurer and by region.

faq.q: How do I find a Medigap plan for my mom in Westchester?
faq.a: Enter her ZIP code in the DFS Medicare Supplement Rate Look-up to see every insurer's monthly rate, then compare the same plan letter across companies. HIICAP (1-800-701-0501) can go over the choices with you for free.

faq.q: My dad in Rochester has a health condition. Can he switch from Medicare Advantage to Medigap?
faq.a: Yes. He can leave Medicare Advantage during open enrollment (October 15 to December 7) or January 1 to March 31, and a New York Medigap insurer must accept him. The policy may have a waiting period of up to six months for pre-existing conditions, shortened by prior coverage with no break over 63 days.

faq.q: Can I still buy Medigap Plan F in New York?
faq.a: Only if you first became eligible for Medicare before January 1, 2020. Plans C, F and F+ are closed to people who became eligible on or after that date.

faq.q: Does Medigap cover prescription drugs?
faq.a: No. Medigap policies sold after 2005 do not include drug coverage, so you need a separate Part D plan. In New York, EPIC can add help on top of Part D for people 65 and older.

title: Memory care in New York: dementia housing, costs and help
seoTitle: Memory care in NY: SNALR, nursing homes, costs, Medicaid
seoDesc: Memory care options for New Yorkers with dementia: SNALRs, nursing homes, adult day and home care, what they cost, where Medicaid fits and free state help.
dek: New York has no license called memory care. Here is what the real options are for a parent with dementia, what they cost by region, where Medicaid helps and the free state programs that support families.
keyFacts: In NY assisted living, serving people with dementia takes a Special Needs Assisted Living Residence (SNALR) certification from the Department of Health.
DOH's voucher eligibility document (updated June 2021) put the average SNALR cost at $10,602 a month in NYC and $9,993 in the Hudson Valley.
DOH may issue up to 200 SNALR vouchers, each covering up to 75% of the regional average private pay rate.
DOH funds 10 Centers of Excellence for Alzheimer's Disease and 10 regional caregiver support programs.
Alzheimer's Association 24-hour helpline, listed by DOH: 1-800-272-3900.
body:
New York does not issue a license called "memory care." The settings that can legally care for someone with dementia are Special Needs Assisted Living Residences (SNALRs), nursing homes, adult day programs and care at home, and each one is paid for differently.

If your mom or dad has just been diagnosed, or the current setup is starting to wobble, this guide walks through each option, what it costs, where Medicaid fits in and the free state-funded dementia help most families never hear about.

What does "memory care" mean in New York?

The New York State Department of Health (DOH) does not license a facility type called memory care. When a residence uses the term, ask which license it holds. The DOH license that covers dementia in assisted living is the Special Needs Assisted Living Residence (SNALR). DOH says a SNALR serves people with special needs, including dementia or other cognitive impairment, under an individualized service plan. A 2016 DOH letter adds that a SNALR must have a special needs plan showing how residents' needs will be safely met, and that one operator can hold both SNALR and Enhanced Assisted Living Residence (EALR) certification.

The other main options are:

SettingWho it fitsMain ways to pay
Care at home (aides, CDPAP)Your parent can stay safely at home with help and supervisionPrivate pay, Medicaid through a managed long term care plan
Social adult day programNeeds supervision during the day; caregiver needs a break or worksPrivate pay, Office for the Aging funding, some MLTC plans
Adult day health careNeeds nursing, therapy or health monitoring during the day but is not homeboundMedicaid managed long term care plans; ask about other ways to pay
Special Needs Assisted Living Residence (SNALR)Needs 24-hour supervision in a residential setting but not continual nursingPrivate pay; limited SNALR voucher program
Nursing homeNeeds 24-hour nursing careMedicaid, private pay; Medicare only for short skilled stays
Ask every "memory care" building one question first. Do you hold a SNALR certification?

How much does memory care cost in New York?

Most dementia care in assisted living is paid privately. Medicare.gov says Medicare and most health insurance, including Medigap, don't pay for long-term care, which includes help with personal tasks like dressing, bathing and using the bathroom.

The clearest state figures on SNALR prices come from DOH's own voucher program. Its eligibility document, last updated in June 2021 and still the one DOH links on the program page, lists these average monthly SNALR costs by region:

Region (counties)Average monthly SNALR cost (DOH, 2021)
New York City (all five boroughs)$10,602
Hudson Valley (Dutchess, Orange, Putnam, Rockland, Sullivan, Ulster, Westchester)$9,993
Long Island (Nassau, Suffolk)$9,089
Capital District (Albany, Saratoga, Schenectady, Rensselaer and others)$7,118
Western New York (Erie, Niagara and others)$6,401
Finger Lakes (Monroe, Ontario and others)$6,079
Central New York (Onondaga, Oneida, Broome and others)$5,939
Northeastern New York (Clinton, Essex, Warren and others)$5,800

These averages come from a document last updated in 2021, so current prices are likely different. Use them to compare regions, and get each residence's actual rates in writing. Ask what the base rate covers and what is billed as extra care.

Is there help paying for a SNALR?

Yes, but it is small. The SNALR Voucher Program for Persons with Dementia, authorized in the 2018-19 State Budget, helps people with Alzheimer's or another dementia stay in assisted living when they can no longer afford private pay. DOH says up to 200 vouchers may be issued, each covering up to 75% of the regional average private pay rate. DOH's FAQs say a resident who can pay 0 to 25% of the monthly fee gets a 75% voucher, 26 to 50% gets 50%, and 51% or more gets 25%.

DOH's eligibility document lists these rules:

  • A diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease or dementia
  • At least 12 months living at the current facility, which must be a participating SNALR
  • Household income at or below the regional standard (for example, $6,274 a month in the Hudson Valley and $7,382 in New York City)
  • Assets no more than six months of the regional average SNALR cost
  • No transfers of assets worth more than three months of that cost in the year before applying
  • Not on Medicaid or Medicaid-eligible, and not receiving SSI (DOH says SSI makes a person Medicaid-eligible)

DOH says that if a waitlist becomes necessary, only eligible applicants are waitlisted, and they are added first come, first served as vouchers become available, program budget permitting. DOH's program page also links a list of participating SNALRs. Email the DOH team at ALTCteam@health.ny.gov to ask about current openings.

Does Medicaid pay for dementia care in New York?

Medicaid pays for a lot of dementia care, mostly at home, in adult day health care and in nursing homes. DOH says people with dementia who can no longer afford to pay privately for a SNALR generally have no option but to enroll in Medicaid, which often means a move to a nursing home. That is why the voucher program exists.

  • At home. Medicaid long-term care at home usually comes through a managed long term care (MLTC) plan. DOH says a person with a dementia or Alzheimer's diagnosis who needs at least supervision with more than one activity of daily living, and needs community care for more than 120 days, meets the needs test for MLTC partial capitation and Medicaid Advantage Plus plans. That can mean home care aides, CDPAP (where a family member or friend can be the paid aide) and adult day health care. See our MLTC guide.
  • PACE. Where it operates, the PACE program gives one team responsibility for primary, acute and long-term care for people 55 and older who need nursing home level care.
  • Assisted Living Program (ALP). For people who medically qualify for a nursing home, Medicaid's ALP pays for services in participating adult homes and enriched housing. Ask whether a building's ALP can serve someone with your parent's level of dementia. See our assisted living guide.
  • Nursing home. Medicaid can pay for long-term nursing home care for people who qualify. DOH notes that MLTC partial capitation plans cover only three months of long-term nursing home care. If a long-term stay runs past three months, New York Medicaid Choice sends a letter saying when your parent will leave the plan, and Medicaid coverage continues outside the plan.

Medicaid has income and asset rules, and nursing home Medicaid looks back at past transfers. Read our Medicaid guide before moving any money.

How do I choose between a SNALR and a nursing home?

The main question is whether your parent needs continual nursing care. Adult care facilities, including SNALRs, are not licensed for continual medical or nursing care, according to DOH. Under the Assisted Living Program rules, residents must not need continual nursing care, be chronically bedfast or be impaired to a degree that endangers other residents.

Talk with your parent's doctor if you see repeated falls, wandering, serious medical problems on top of dementia, or a need for constant hands-on help. Ask each nursing home whether it has a dedicated dementia unit and how it is staffed. Check each one's star ratings and inspections with our nursing home ratings guide.

  1. Get a clear diagnosis. New York funds ten Centers of Excellence for Alzheimer's Disease (CEADs) for diagnosis and management of dementia. A clear diagnosis helps you match the setting to the stage.
  2. List what your parent needs now. Supervision only, help with bathing and dressing, medication management, or nursing care.
  3. Check licenses. On NYS Health Profiles, search by county and the service "Special Needs Assisted Living Residence". For nursing homes, see our nursing home ratings guide.
  4. Ask about the next stage. What would make a resident leave? Does the building also hold EALR certification, so physical decline doesn't force a move?
  5. Visit more than once. Watch how staff redirect residents who are upset. Ask about staffing at night and on weekends.
  6. Sort out the paperwork. A health care proxy and power of attorney are far easier to sign while your parent can still understand them. If that window has closed, see our guardianship guide.

What free dementia help does New York offer families?

DOH funds three programs that cover regions across the state. Find the one for your county on the DOH Alzheimer's programs by county page.

  • Centers of Excellence for Alzheimer's Disease (CEADs). Ten regional centers for diagnosis and management of dementia. They refer families to community support and promote research and clinical trials.
  • Alzheimer's Disease Community Assistance Program (ADCAP). Run by seven Alzheimer's Association chapters in New York. Services include a 24-hour helpline, care planning, caregiver education and support groups. The 24-hour helpline is 1-800-272-3900.
  • Alzheimer's Disease Regional Caregiver Support Initiative. Ten regional organizations offering caregiver assessments, support groups, education, wellness programs and respite. DOH says respite can include overnight stays.

The New York State Office for the Aging (NYSOFA) adds more. NYSOFA says Area Agencies on Aging (county Offices for the Aging, and NYC Aging in the five boroughs) offer services like transportation, meals, personal care and legal help, and support caregivers directly with programs such as respite. NYSOFA also offers a free New York Caregiver Portal with training and support for unpaid caregivers. Call NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871 and name your parent's county to be routed to local help. Our caregiver support guide and adult day care guide go further.

If your parent already lives in a facility

The Long Term Care Ombudsman Program advocates for residents of nursing homes and licensed adult care homes, including assisted living. Call 1-855-582-6769. Complaints about an assisted living residence go to DOH at 1-866-893-6772.

faq.q: How do I find memory care for my dad in Rockland County?
faq.a: Search NYS Health Profiles: Adult Care Facilities for Rockland County and the service Special Needs Assisted Living Residence. A residence needs SNALR certification to serve people with dementia. For nursing homes, see our nursing home ratings guide and ask each home how it cares for residents with dementia.

faq.q: Will Medicaid pay for my mom's memory care in Brooklyn?
faq.a: Medicaid can pay for home care, CDPAP and adult day health care through a managed long term care plan, for services in a participating Assisted Living Program, and for long-term nursing home care if she qualifies. DOH says people who can no longer pay privately for a SNALR generally have to turn to Medicaid, which often means a move to a nursing home. The SNALR voucher program was created to prevent that. Ask HRA about Medicaid in Brooklyn.

faq.q: What is a SNALR in New York?
faq.a: A Special Needs Assisted Living Residence is an assisted living residence with a DOH certificate to serve people with special needs, most commonly Alzheimer's disease or other dementia. It must have a special needs plan showing how residents' needs will be safely met.

faq.q: How much does memory care cost in New York?
faq.a: DOH's SNALR voucher eligibility document, last updated June 2021, listed average monthly SNALR costs from $5,800 in Northeastern New York to $10,602 in New York City. Prices have likely changed, so get written rates from each residence.

faq.q: Who qualifies for the SNALR voucher program?
faq.a: DOH lists a dementia diagnosis, at least 12 months at the current facility in a participating SNALR, income and assets under regional limits, no large transfers in the year before applying, and not being on Medicaid or SSI. Up to 200 vouchers may be issued, and a waitlist may apply.

faq.q: Where can I get free help caring for a parent with dementia in New York?
faq.a: DOH funds Centers of Excellence for Alzheimer's Disease, Alzheimer's Association community programs with a 24-hour helpline at 1-800-272-3900, and regional caregiver support programs with respite. NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871 links you to local services in your county.

title: Nursing home ratings in New York: stars, inspections, staffing
seoTitle: How to Read NY Nursing Home Ratings
seoDesc: Read Medicare star ratings, NY inspection reports and staffing rules, spot Special Focus Facilities, and know who to call about a New York nursing home.
dek: How Medicare's five-star ratings work, where to find New York inspection and staffing records, how nursing home bills get paid and who to call when something goes wrong.
keyFacts: Inspection stars are graded within each state: the top 10% of New York homes get five stars and the bottom 20% get one.
New York requires 3.5 hours of care per resident per day, including at least 2.2 from aides and 1.1 from licensed nurses.
Medicare covers up to 100 days of skilled nursing care. Days 21 to 100 cost $222 a day in 2027.
Medicaid reviews asset transfers made in the 60 months before applying for nursing home care.
Ombudsman: 1-855-582-6769. DOH nursing home complaints: 1-888-201-4563.
body:
Start with Medicare's Care Compare website, which rates almost every nursing home in New York from one to five stars, then check the state's own Nursing Home Profiles for inspection and enforcement history. Neither source tells the whole story alone, so use both and then visit in person.

If something goes wrong after your mom or dad moves in, New York has two places to call. The Long Term Care Ombudsman Program advocates for residents at 1-855-582-6769. The Department of Health (DOH) takes nursing home complaints at 1-888-201-4563. Below is how to read each rating, what the staffing rules are, how the bills get paid and what to ask on a tour.

What do the Medicare star ratings mean?

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) gives each certified nursing home an overall rating plus three separate ratings. Five stars means much above average. One star means much below average. You can search by town, county or ZIP code on Medicare Care Compare.

RatingWhat it measures
Health inspectionsProblems found in the two most recent standard state inspections, plus complaint and infection control inspections from the last three years. Recent findings count more.
StaffingNurse and aide hours per resident, registered nurse (RN) hours, weekend staffing, nurse turnover and administrator departures.
Quality measuresHow residents are doing on things like falls, pressure ulcers and the ability to get around, for both long-stay residents and short-stay rehab patients.
OverallStarts from the inspection rating and moves up or down based on staffing and quality.

The inspection stars are graded on a curve inside each state. According to the CMS technical guide, the top 10 percent of homes in New York get five stars, the bottom 20 percent get one star, and the middle 70 percent are split about evenly across two, three and four stars. So a three-star home is roughly average for New York. That matters if you are comparing a home in Rockland County with one across the line in New Jersey, where the curve is different.

How is the overall rating worked out?

Inspections carry the most weight because trained surveyors actually walked the halls. The other two ratings can only nudge the result.

  1. Start with inspections. A home with three inspection stars starts at three.
  2. Adjust for staffing. Five staffing stars add one star. One staffing star takes one away.
  3. Adjust for quality. Five quality stars add one star. One quality star takes one away.
  4. Apply the limits. The result stays between one and five. A home with one inspection star can rise by one star at most, however good its other numbers are.

Because of those rules, always open the three separate ratings. A four-star home with two inspection stars is a very different place from a four-star home with four inspection stars.

Look for three symbols on a home's page.

  • Abuse icon. Marks homes cited for abuse. These homes are capped at two inspection stars, so four stars overall is the most they can show.
  • Yellow warning sign. Shows for homes in the Special Focus Facility program. They get no star ratings while they are in it.
  • Trophy icon. Described in the September 2026 CMS guide. It appears next to the stars of high performers, homes with fewer citations and higher staffing.
The overall star can hide a weak inspection record. Open all three ratings every time.

Where can I read New York inspection reports?

Use the state's NYS Nursing Home Profiles website, run by DOH. It covers every nursing home in New York and lets you search by region or county, by service, alphabetically or by enforcement actions. You can compare homes side by side and print a directory.

Each profile shows inspection and complaint results and quality scores on care, quality of life, resident safety and prevention. The "Search by Enforcements" tool is worth a few minutes. It shows homes the state has fined or acted against.

When you read an inspection report, look past the number of citations.

  • Harm. Citations where a resident was actually hurt, or put in immediate danger, matter far more than paperwork problems.
  • Repeats. The same problem cited inspection after inspection (falls, bed sores, medication errors) means it is not getting fixed.
  • Complaints. Several substantiated complaints in a short stretch tell you families have been calling the state.
  • Timing. A bad year followed by two clean inspections is a different story from a recent slide.

Ask the administrator about anything that worries you. A good home will tell you what happened and what changed.

How do I check staffing at a New York nursing home?

Check the staffing stars and hours on Care Compare, then ask the home directly. New York has its own minimum. Under the state's staffing law, every nursing home must provide at least 3.5 hours of care per resident per day from aides and nurses.

New York staffing ruleMinimum per resident per day
Total care from certified nurse aides, licensed practical nurses and RNs3.5 hours
From certified nurse aidesAt least 2.2 hours
From licensed nursesAt least 1.1 hours

The rules are posted on the DOH minimum staffing page. On Care Compare, the staffing rating also looks at turnover. High turnover means residents keep meeting new faces, which is hard on people with dementia. Weekend staffing gets its own score too, so check it. Visit on a Saturday afternoon if you can.

What is a Special Focus Facility?

It is a federal program for nursing homes with a long record of serious problems. A home in the program gets a full inspection at least once every six months. To leave the program, it has to pass two standard inspections in a row with 12 or fewer deficiencies and none above a set severity.

CMS posts the list every month, along with a list of candidates, the homes in each state with the worst records that could be added. On the October 28, 2026 list, three New York homes were in the program and 15 New York homes were named as candidates.

Being a candidate is a warning sign. The home is still open and admitting residents. If a home on either list is the only one near family, visit several times, talk to other families, read the latest inspections and call the ombudsman before you decide.

Who pays for a nursing home in New York?

For most families it is a mix of Medicare for short rehab stays, then personal savings, then Medicaid. Knowing which one applies avoids surprise bills.

PayerWhat it covers in 2027
Medicare Part AShort-term skilled nursing or rehab after a hospital stay of at least 3 inpatient days in a row. Up to 100 days per benefit period. Days 1 to 20 cost $0 a day after the Part A deductible ($1,776 in 2027). Days 21 to 100 cost $222 a day. From day 101 you pay everything.
MedicaidLong-term care for as long as it is needed, if your parent meets income and asset rules. A resident on Medicaid keeps $50 a month as a personal needs allowance.
Private payRates are not regulated by the state. The home must give 30 days' written notice before a rate increase and can ask for no more than three months' prepayment.

The Medicare figures come from the Medicare skilled nursing page and the CMS 2027 fact sheet. Time spent "under observation" or in the emergency room does not count toward the three days, so ask the hospital if your parent is formally admitted. Medicare nursing home coverage is short-term skilled care, so plan for what comes after.

For Medicaid, the state reviews money and property transferred in the 60 months before the application. Gifts in that window can delay coverage. In New York City, apply through the Human Resources Administration (HRA) at 718-557-1399. Elsewhere, apply through your county Department of Social Services. DOH also notes that Medicaid residents 21 and older in a long-term nursing home stay must stay in or join a managed care plan. Those who also have Medicare must join a Managed Long Term Care plan. DOH suggests seeing an elder law attorney before admission. The New York State Bar Association lawyer referral line is 1-800-342-3661. For the full rules, see our guide to Medicaid for older adults in New York.

What should I ask when I visit?

Ratings tell you about the past. A visit tells you about today. Go at least twice, once unannounced and once at a meal.

  • How many aides and nurses work each shift on the unit where my parent would live, including nights and weekends?
  • How many of your aides come from staffing agencies, and how long have your core staff been here?
  • What did your last inspection find, and what did you change?
  • Who is the doctor, how often do they see residents, and who covers nights?
  • How do you prevent falls and pressure sores? How do you handle a resident who wanders?
  • How do you tell families about a fall, a new medication or a change in condition?
  • What happens if my parent runs out of money and moves to Medicaid? Will they keep their room?
  • Is there an active resident council and family council? Can I talk to a family member?

Watch how staff talk to residents. Notice smells, call lights left blinking and whether people are up and dressed. Trust what you see. DOH says a caring home should welcome both your visits and your questions.

Who do I call if something goes wrong?

Start with the staff and the administrator. If that does not fix it, or if someone is in danger, go outside the building.

  1. Call the ombudsman. The Long Term Care Ombudsman Program advocates for residents of nursing homes and adult care homes, investigates complaints and helps sort out problems with staff. Call 1-855-582-6769 or find your local ombudsman by county.
  2. File a complaint with DOH. Call the Nursing Home Complaint and Discharge Appeal Hotline at 1-888-201-4563. You can call any time and leave a message. Staff answer weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. DOH asks that complaints be submitted in writing, so you can also use the online complaint form.
  3. Call 911 for emergencies. If you think a resident is in immediate danger, call 911 first, then report it to DOH.
  4. Keep notes. Write down dates, names, what you saw and who you told. Photos help.

The same hotline handles appeals if a home tries to discharge or transfer your parent against their wishes. Ask for the discharge notice in writing.

Related guides: NY Connects for help finding long-term care, PACE in New York as an option for staying at home, and hospice care in New York.

faq.q: How do I check a nursing home's inspection record for my mom in Buffalo?
faq.a: Look the home up on Medicare Care Compare and open the Inspections tab, then search the NYS Nursing Home Profiles site (profiles.health.ny.gov) by Erie County. Profiles shows state inspection results, complaints and enforcement actions. Focus on citations where residents were harmed and on problems that repeat.

faq.q: My dad is in rehab at a nursing home in Brooklyn after a hospital stay. How long will Medicare pay?
faq.a: Medicare Part A covers up to 100 days of skilled nursing or rehab per benefit period if he had at least 3 inpatient days in a row first and still needs daily skilled care. Days 1 to 20 cost $0 a day once the Part A deductible ($1,776 in 2027) is paid. Days 21 to 100 cost $222 a day in 2027. Coverage stops sooner if he no longer needs skilled care.

faq.q: What is the minimum staffing a New York nursing home must have?
faq.a: State law requires at least 3.5 hours of care per resident per day from certified nurse aides, licensed practical nurses and registered nurses. At least 2.2 of those hours must come from aides and at least 1.1 from licensed nurses.

faq.q: What does a yellow warning sign on Care Compare mean?
faq.a: It means the home is in the federal Special Focus Facility program for homes with a history of serious quality problems. These homes are inspected at least every six months and do not get star ratings while in the program.

faq.q: How much money can my parent keep after Medicaid starts paying for a nursing home?
faq.a: A Medicaid resident in a New York nursing home keeps $50 a month as a personal needs allowance. Most other income goes toward the cost of care. Ask your county Department of Social Services, or HRA in New York City, about the rules for a spouse still living at home.

faq.q: Who do I call to complain about a nursing home in New York?
faq.a: Call the DOH Nursing Home Complaint Hotline at 1-888-201-4563 or use the online complaint form. For help advocating for a resident, call the Long Term Care Ombudsman Program at 1-855-582-6769. If someone is in danger, call 911 first.

title: NY Connects: where New Yorkers start for long-term care help
seoTitle: NY Connects: free help finding long-term care in NY
seoDesc: NY Connects is New York's free front door for home care, meals, rides and Medicaid help. The number to call, how NYC differs and what to have ready first.
dek: One free phone number links your family to home care, meals, transportation and help applying for Medicaid. Here is what NY Connects does, how it works in New York City and upstate, and how to get the most out of the first call.
keyFacts: NY Connects statewide number: 1-800-342-9871. It routes you to your local office by county.
The service is free and unbiased, and it serves older adults and people with disabilities of any age, on any type of payment.
In the five boroughs, NYC Aging runs NY Connects through one partner agency per borough.
NY Connects can help you apply for public benefits such as Medicaid and SNAP.
Medicaid home care assessments are scheduled through the New York Independent Assessor at 1-855-222-8350.
body:
NY Connects is New York State's free, unbiased starting point for long-term services and supports, like home care, meals, rides and help applying for Medicaid. Call 1-800-342-9871 and you will be connected to the NY Connects office for the county where your parent lives.

It is meant for the moment when something has changed. Maybe your dad is coming home from the hospital, your mom stopped driving, or one parent can no longer care for the other alone. NY Connects helps you figure out what exists nearby, what your family may qualify for and who to call next.

What is NY Connects, and who runs it?

NY Connects is what the state calls a No Wrong Door system. The idea is simple. No matter which agency you call first, you should end up with the right help. The New York State Office for the Aging (NYSOFA) oversees it. Local partners run it day to day.

Those local partners are:

  • Area Agencies on Aging, which are the county Offices for the Aging outside New York City and NYC Aging in the five boroughs.
  • Independent Living Centers, six regional centers that focus on people with disabilities.
  • Local Departments of Social Services, the county offices that handle Medicaid and other public benefits.

NY Connects serves older adults and people with disabilities of all ages. It also helps the family members, caregivers and professionals who call on their behalf. It serves people no matter how they pay, privately, through public programs or a mix of both. You can get help by phone, online, in person or by email.

You do not need to know the name of the program you need. You only need to describe what is going wrong at home.

What can NY Connects actually do for my parent?

The state describes four parts to the service. Two matter most to families.

Information and assistance

A trained specialist listens to your situation and links you to services in your area. Typical examples include home care, home delivered meals and transportation. They can also help you work out if your parent may be eligible for public benefits such as Medicaid or the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), and help with the application.

Person-centered options counseling

This is a longer, goal-driven conversation. The specialist looks at your parent's preferences, needs and resources, then lays out the choices. The result may be a written action plan. It is a good fit when the family is weighing several paths, such as more help at home, a move closer to family or assisted living.

Public education and Long Term Care Councils

NY Connects also runs outreach so people know that long-term care can happen outside a nursing home. Counties have Long Term Care Councils of consumers, caregivers, providers and officials that recommends improvements to the local system.

How do I reach NY Connects in New York City?

In the five boroughs, NY Connects is administered by the New York City Department for the Aging (NYC Aging) and funded by NYSOFA. NYC Aging contracts with one agency in each borough. You can call the statewide number or go straight to the borough office.

BoroughNY Connects partnerPhone
BronxNeighborhood SHOPP347-862-5200
BrooklynPSS718-671-6200
ManhattanHudson Guild212-966-9852
QueensSelfhelp Community Services718-559-4400
Staten IslandCommunity Agency for Senior Citizens718-489-3954
CitywideNY Connects statewide line1-800-342-9871

NYC Aging says hours vary by borough. They are generally weekdays from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., with one evening until 7 p.m. You can also email NYConnects@aging.nyc.gov. If you are deaf or hard of hearing, use the NY Relay System at 711.

NYC Aging also runs Aging Connect, its information and referral center for older adults and families, at 212-244-6469 (212-AGING-NYC). For other City programs, call 311. Both lines can point you to senior centers, case management and other city services. See the NYC Aging NY Connects page for current details.

How does it work outside New York City?

Everywhere else in the state, the statewide number routes you to the NY Connects office for your county. In most counties that office sits inside, or works closely with, the county Office for the Aging. The local Department of Social Services handles the Medicaid side.

Say your mom lives in Utica and you live in Brooklyn. Call 1-800-342-9871 and ask for the office that serves her county, not yours. Services follow where the person receiving care lives. The NY Connects website also has a searchable directory of providers and local offices.

Many county offices can also tell you about state-funded help for people who are not on Medicaid. One example is the Expanded In-home Services for the Elderly Program (EISEP). Our EISEP guide explains it.

What happens if my parent needs Medicaid home care?

NY Connects can explain the options and help start a Medicaid application. The medical assessment that decides whether Medicaid will pay for personal care at home is a separate step. It is done by the New York Independent Assessor Program (NYIAP), which the state Department of Health contracts out to Maximus.

  1. Confirm Medicaid. Medicaid home care requires Medicaid, so apply first if your parent does not have it. In NYC, Medicaid is handled by the Human Resources Administration (HRA). Elsewhere, it is your county Department of Social Services. NY Connects can help with the forms. Our Medicaid guide covers income and asset rules.
  2. Request the assessment. Your parent, or an authorized representative on file, can call the NYIAP helpline at 1-855-222-8350 (TTY 1-888-329-1541) to ask for an initial assessment. If your parent is already in a Medicaid managed care plan, call the plan instead.
  3. Do the Community Health Assessment. This visit usually takes 2 to 3 hours. You can choose in person or video.
  4. Do the clinical appointment. A separate appointment of up to 1 hour with a clinician, also in person or by video.
  5. Choose how care is delivered. If your parent qualifies, the next step may be choosing a managed long-term care plan through New York Medicaid Choice at 1-888-401-6582, or using home care through Medicaid directly.

If your parent is not in a health plan and has an urgent need, the Department of Health says to contact the local Department of Social Services. Staff there will call NYIAP with you to schedule.

After a hospital stay

If your parent is still in the hospital or rehab, ask for the discharge planner or social worker before leaving. They can start referrals for short-term home health, which works differently from long-term Medicaid home care. Our home care agencies guide explains the difference.

What should I have ready before I call?

A first call goes faster when you have the basics in front of you. You do not need every item, but each one helps.

  • Your parent's address and county. Help is organized by where they live.
  • Insurance cards. Medicare, Medicaid if any, and any Medicare Advantage or Medigap plan.
  • A short list of what is hard right now. Bathing, dressing, meals, medications, stairs, getting to appointments, being alone at night.
  • Recent changes. A fall, a hospital stay, a new diagnosis, memory changes.
  • Who helps now. Which family members or neighbors pitch in and how many hours a week.
  • Rough monthly income and savings. This shapes which programs fit. You can give a ballpark.
  • Legal papers, if you have them. A health care proxy or power of attorney lets you act more easily. See our power of attorney guide and health care proxy and MOLST guide.

What should I ask for on the first call?

Specialists are there to help, but you get more when you ask direct questions. Try these:

  • Which services in my parent's county could help with the problems I described?
  • Could my parent qualify for Medicaid, or for help that is not Medicaid?
  • Can you help us fill out the Medicaid application, or tell us who can?
  • Is there a waiting list for any of these programs?
  • Can we set up options counseling to compare our choices?
  • Are there caregiver supports for me, like respite or support groups? Our caregiver support guide lists more.
  • Who do I call next, and what should I bring?

Write down the name of the person you spoke with and any reference number. If you are juggling calls for a parent in another county, keep one notebook or phone note for everything.

What mistakes do families make?

  • Calling the office near you instead of near your parent. Services follow your parent's address.
  • Waiting for a crisis. Medicaid applications and assessments take time. Start the conversation when you first notice your parent struggling.
  • Assuming Medicare will cover long-term help. Medicare does not provide long-term or custodial care unless medical care is needed. Our Medicare costs guide has the 2027 figures.
  • Hiring the first person who answers an ad. When someone will come into your parent's home, check licenses and background first.
  • Not asking about family caregiver pay. If your parent has Medicaid, a relative may be able to be paid through the Consumer Directed Personal Assistance Program. See our CDPAP guide.

NY Connects will not push a particular agency or product. That makes it a good first call before you talk to anyone selling something.

faq.q: What is the NY Connects phone number?
faq.a: Call 1-800-342-9871. The statewide line connects you to the NY Connects office for the county where the person needing help lives. In New York City, you can also call the borough partner directly.

faq.q: How do I get home care help for my mom in Queens?
faq.a: Call NY Connects in Queens, run by Selfhelp Community Services for NYC Aging, at 718-559-4400, or the statewide line at 1-800-342-9871. If she has Medicaid and needs personal care, the assessment is scheduled through the New York Independent Assessor at 1-855-222-8350.

faq.q: My dad lives in Buffalo and I live in Manhattan. Who do I call?
faq.a: Call 1-800-342-9871 and ask for the NY Connects office that serves Erie County, where your dad lives. Services are arranged by the older adult's address, so the Manhattan office will send you to his county.

faq.q: Does NY Connects cost anything?
faq.a: No. NY Connects is free and unbiased information and assistance. Some services it refers you to may have costs or eligibility rules, and the specialist can explain those.

faq.q: Does my parent have to be on Medicaid to use NY Connects?
faq.a: No. NY Connects serves people regardless of how they pay, privately, through public programs or both. It can also help you find out if your parent could qualify for Medicaid and help with the application.

faq.q: Is NY Connects only for older adults?
faq.a: No. It serves older adults and people with disabilities of all ages, plus their families, caregivers and the professionals who help them.
