title: PACE in New York: all-in-one care for older adults at home
seoTitle: PACE in New York: who qualifies, costs and where it runs
seoDesc: PACE puts doctors, home care, drugs and rides into one plan for New Yorkers 55 and up. Who qualifies, what it costs and which NY counties have a program.
dek: PACE, a Medicare and Medicaid program, gives one team responsibility for nearly all of your parent's care, so they can stay at home instead of moving to a nursing home. It runs only in certain counties. Here is how it works in New York.
keyFacts: PACE is for people 55 and older who need a nursing home level of care but can live safely at home with help.
PACE covers all Medicare and Medicaid covered services, including prescription drugs, plus other care the PACE team decides is needed.
With Medicaid there is no monthly PACE premium, and approved care has no deductible, copay or coinsurance.
NY DOH lists 10 PACE programs, operating in 25 counties including all five boroughs.
New York Medicaid Choice helps with managed long-term care enrollment: 1-888-401-6582.
body:
The Program of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE) is a health plan for people 55 and older who need nursing home level care but want to stay at home, and in New York it is available only in certain counties. One team of doctors, nurses, social workers and therapists manages almost everything, from checkups and drugs to home care and rides.

For a family worn out by juggling specialists, aides and pharmacies, that can be a relief. It also means your parent agrees to get care through the PACE team. This guide explains who qualifies, what it costs and where it runs.

Who qualifies for PACE in New York?

The New York State Department of Health (DOH) lists these requirements for PACE through Medicaid:

  • Age 55 or older
  • Live in the PACE program's service area
  • Have Medicaid. If your parent also has Medicare, they need Part A and Part B and must enroll in the program's aligned Medicare plan.
  • Be able to stay in, or return to, home and community without risk to health and safety
  • Need a nursing home level of care
  • Need at least one community-based long-term care service for more than 120 days

Medicare.gov describes the same core rules nationally: 55 or older, living in a PACE service area, certified by the state as needing nursing home level care and able to live safely in the community with PACE's help.

Needing a nursing home level of care does not mean your parent must move into one. Many PACE members have trouble with several daily activities, memory loss or chronic conditions and still live at home.

PACE gives one team the whole picture. The trade is that your parent uses that team's doctors.

What does PACE cover?

According to Medicare.gov, PACE covers all Medicare and Medicaid covered services, plus other care the PACE team decides your parent needs. That includes prescription drugs. Services Medicare.gov lists include:

  • Adult day care
  • Dental care
  • Home care
  • Hospital care
  • Therapy
  • Transportation to appointments
  • Nursing home care when it is medically necessary

DOH describes the PACE plan as covering all medically necessary services, including primary, acute and long-term care, coordinated by one team.

A warning about drug plans

If your parent has Medicare, PACE provides their Part D drug coverage. Medicare.gov says joining a separate Medicare drug plan will disenroll them from PACE. Be careful during Medicare open enrollment not to sign up for another plan by mistake.

How much does PACE cost?

Your parent hasWhat they pay (per Medicare.gov)
Medicaid (with or without Medicare)No monthly PACE premium
Medicare onlyA monthly premium for the long-term care part of PACE, plus a separate premium for Part D drugs
Neither Medicare nor MedicaidCan pay the PACE premium privately
Any of the aboveNo deductible, copayment or coinsurance for drugs and care the PACE team approves

Medicare.gov does not publish dollar amounts for private premiums, because each program sets its own. Ask the program directly. Note that the DOH page describes PACE through Medicaid, while the DOH plan directory says PACE can be paid by Medicaid, Medicare or private pay. If your parent is not on Medicaid, ask each program how enrollment works for them.

If your parent's income or savings are close to the Medicaid limits, read our Medicaid guide first. Help with Medicare costs is in our Medicare Savings Program guide.

Where does PACE operate in New York?

The DOH Managed Long Term Care Plan Directory (revised January 2026) lists these 10 PACE programs, in 25 counties. Counties not on this list have no PACE program in the directory.

PACE programCounties listed by DOH
ArchCare Senior LifeBronx, Manhattan, Staten Island, Rockland, Westchester
Centerlight Healthcare PACEBronx, Brooklyn, Manhattan, Queens, Staten Island, Nassau, Suffolk, Westchester
Catholic Health LifeErie
Complete Senior CareNiagara
Eddy Senior CareAlbany, Rensselaer, Schenectady
ElderONEMonroe, Ontario, Wayne
Fallon Health Weinberg PACEErie, Niagara
PACE at Hudson HeadwatersSaratoga, Warren, Washington
PACE CNYCayuga, Chautauqua, Onondaga
Total Senior CareAllegany, Cattaraugus, Chautauqua

Service areas can be smaller than a whole county, so confirm your parent's ZIP code with the program. Check the current DOH plan directory before you call, since it can change. Medicare.gov's PACE page also lets you search for PACE plans in your area.

If your parent lives in a county with no PACE program, other managed long-term care plans or Medicaid home care may fit. See our home care agencies guide and CDPAP guide.

How do I enroll my parent in PACE?

  1. Check the county. Confirm a PACE program serves your parent's address using the table above and the DOH directory.
  2. Call the program. Ask for an intake visit. Ask about the PACE center your parent would attend, how rides work and which doctors they would see.
  3. Sort out Medicaid. If your parent does not have Medicaid yet, apply through HRA in New York City or the county Department of Social Services elsewhere. NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871 can help.
  4. Complete the assessment. Your parent must be assessed as needing a nursing home level of care and as able to live safely at home with PACE's help. Ask the program which assessments it will arrange.
  5. Get enrollment help. New York Medicaid Choice, which helps people choose and enroll in managed long-term care plans including PACE, is at 1-888-401-6582 (TTY 1-888-329-1541).
  6. Review the enrollment agreement. Read it with your parent. Ask what happens with current doctors, home aides and pharmacies.

DOH also takes managed long-term care questions by email at MLTCInfo@health.ny.gov.

What is daily life like in PACE?

PACE is built around a team and, usually, a PACE center. Medicare.gov says a team of health care professionals coordinates your parent's care. DOH describes that team as doctors, nurses, social workers and other professionals who manage Medicare, Medicaid, long-term care and drug benefits under one plan.

In practice, that changes a few things for a family:

  • One place to call. When something changes, you call the PACE team instead of separate offices for the doctor, the aide and the pharmacy.
  • The team decides what is needed. Care beyond the usual Medicare and Medicaid list can be added if the team decides your parent needs it.
  • Transportation is part of the plan. Rides to appointments are covered, which matters a great deal after your parent stops driving.
  • Care follows your parent's needs. If your parent later needs a nursing home and it is medically necessary, PACE covers it.

Say your mom lives in Schenectady, has diabetes and early memory loss, and no longer drives. She might spend part of some weekdays at the PACE center, see her primary doctor there, get her medicines through the plan and have an aide come to the house on other days. The exact plan depends on her assessment and the team.

How is PACE different from other managed long-term care plans?

DOH lists three kinds of managed long-term care plans in New York.

Plan typeMinimum ageCoverage neededWhat it covers
MLTC Partial Capitation18MedicaidCommunity-based long-term care and some extra services, including home care and up to 3 months of nursing home care
Medicaid Advantage Plus (MAP)18Medicaid and MedicarePrimary, acute, behavioral health and long-term care together
PACE55Medicaid, Medicare or private payAll medically necessary primary, acute and long-term care, through the PACE team

For Partial Capitation and MAP plans, DOH requires a need for community-based long-term care for more than 120 days plus the minimum needs rules. For PACE, DOH requires the 120 days and a nursing home level of care.

What should we ask before joining?

  • Which doctors and hospitals will my parent use? Can they keep any current doctors?
  • How often will my parent go to the PACE center, and how long are the rides?
  • How many hours of home care could they get, and who decides?
  • What happens in an emergency, at night or on weekends?
  • How do we appeal a decision we disagree with?
  • How does leaving PACE work if it is not a good fit?
  • What is the monthly cost if my parent does not have Medicaid?

What mistakes do families make?

  • Signing up for a separate Part D plan. It ends PACE enrollment.
  • Seeing outside doctors without checking. Care goes through the PACE team. Ask before booking anything.
  • Assuming PACE is everywhere. Many New York counties have no program.
  • Waiting too long. Joining sooner gives your parent more time to use the day center and therapies while they can still benefit.

faq.q: Is there a PACE program for my mom in Brooklyn?
faq.a: Yes. The DOH plan directory lists Centerlight Healthcare PACE in Kings County (Brooklyn). Call the program to confirm it serves her address and to set up an intake visit.

faq.q: Can my dad join PACE in Rochester?
faq.a: The DOH directory lists ElderONE for Monroe County, which includes Rochester. He must be 55 or older, need a nursing home level of care and be able to live safely at home with PACE's help.

faq.q: How much does PACE cost with Medicaid in New York?
faq.a: Medicare.gov says people with Medicaid pay no monthly PACE premium, and there is no deductible, copay or coinsurance for care and drugs the PACE team approves.

faq.q: Can someone with only Medicare join PACE?
faq.a: Medicare.gov says people with Medicare but not Medicaid pay a monthly premium for the long-term care portion and a premium for Part D drugs. Ask the New York PACE program in your area how enrollment works without Medicaid.

faq.q: Does PACE include prescription drugs?
faq.a: Yes. PACE covers prescription drugs, and for people with Medicare it provides Part D coverage. Joining a separate Medicare drug plan will disenroll your parent from PACE.

faq.q: Does my parent have to go to a nursing home to use PACE?
faq.a: No. PACE is for people who need a nursing home level of care but can live safely at home with PACE's help. PACE covers nursing home care only when it is medically necessary.
